text:
A Constitutional and Factual Concern Regarding the Dissolution of the Family Federation

The dissolution of the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification raises important questions concerning both religious freedom and whether all materially relevant facts were sufficiently examined.

On March 4, 2026, the Tokyo High Court upheld the dissolution order, and on June 22, 2026, the Supreme Court dismissed the Federation’s special appeal, allowing the order to become final. The judicial decisions addressed alleged unlawful conduct, including the solicitation of donations under circumstances said to have impaired individuals’ freedom of decision-making.

At the same time, other allegations deserve careful examination. In May 2024, Satoshi Hamada, then a member of the House of Councillors, submitted a formal inquiry concerning allegations of abduction, confinement, and forced religious deconversion involving Family Federation members. The government responded that criminal conduct would be addressed strictly according to law and evidence, while explaining that its dissolution request was based on seven rounds of reporting requests and interviews with relevant persons.

These records do not establish that every allegation of forced deconversion is true. They do establish, however, that such allegations were formally raised before the Diet and required governmental consideration. In a constitutional democracy, serious allegations should neither be dismissed without examination nor treated as established facts without sufficient evidence.

There is also significant disagreement within the Christian community. The United Church of Christ in Japan supported the government’s dissolution request and subsequently supported the Tokyo High Court decision, while expressly acknowledging that Article 20 continues to protect the religious activities of individual members. In 2023, several major Christian organizations likewise issued a joint statement supporting dissolution.

This demonstrates that substantial Christian support for dissolution existed, but it also shows why the constitutional issue should not be reduced to whether the Family Federation’s beliefs are acceptable to other Christians.

Articles 19 and 20 of the Constitution protect freedom of thought, conscience, and religion, while Article 31 protects personal liberty through legally established procedures. Where confinement, coercion, or interference with religious decision-making is alleged, these constitutional protections provide an important framework for examining the facts.

Pastor Haruhisa Nakagawa has offered a different perspective based on his reported experience of entering the organization and examining its activities. He argues that the central ethical emphasis of the Unification Principle includes living for the sake of others and loving one’s enemies. His testimony should not be treated as conclusive, but it represents a perspective that can be considered alongside testimony from critics and former members.

The essential point is the need to distinguish between religious doctrine, organizational conduct, and individual misconduct. A religious teaching cannot automatically be equated with every action of an individual member, just as allegations of unlawful conduct should not be accepted without evidence.

The constitutional concern, therefore, is not whether the Family Federation should be regarded favorably or unfavorably. It is whether all materially relevant evidence—including evidence that challenges the prevailing narrative—has been examined with equal seriousness.

The courts should determine the legality of specific conduct on the basis of evidence and law, rather than determine the legitimacy of a religious worldview according to social or theological preference.

That distinction is essential to preserving both the rule of law and freedom of religion in Japan.

text:
A vital principle for Baptists is that freedom of conscience is a meaningless concession if it does not extend to "freedom of act." Many before had offered religious toleration or liberty of conscience, but still coerced religious acts. Baptists militated against this.

More from the Coldwater Association's Centennial Report in 1874:

"[Our fathers] contested every inch of ground in the hard, unequal struggle with Priest, Magistrate and Statesman, for the inalienable, God-conferred rights of man—freedom of act, of conscience, in choosing a form of worship and the pursuits of happiness. To express these inalienable rights, they used the very significant phrase, "Soul Liberty"—denied the right of the Magistrate to coerce in matters of religion.

God gave them the victory after a long and painful conflict, in which they endured every species of indignity and suffering that ingenuity could invent and power inflict; as whipping, inciting of mobs, imprisonment in county jails, fines, amounting sometimes to more property than they possessed, and banishment under penalty of death.

The victories which they won, were victories for the world. The principles contended for were not stumbled upon, but plainly taught in God's inspired Word and form an article of faith in the creed of Baptists of all ages. . . the name of Baptist should be the synonym of the broadest civil and religious liberty.

But while they left us in possession of this rich heritage, it is not a peaceful possession. We have battles to fight."

text:
Many years ago, I exchanged letters with an atheist. In the course of our discussion, he made two statements about how the God of Christians was “unfair.”

It isn’t fair, he insisted, that God limits human freedom by imposing rules against various actions and desires.

And it also isn’t fair, he wrote, that God has allowed pain, suffering, and evil in this world. A good God, he argued, wouldn’t allow such things.

It was an example of having one’s cake and eating it, too. Or of having one’s sin and also ignoring the consequences.

Yes, the existence of evil is indeed perplexing, “as painful as it is mysterious,” says the Catechism. But the Christian faith, understood correctly, “constitutes the answer to this question” (CCC, par 309). It is part of the “drama of sin” in which free creatures can either accept or reject the Creator’s gift of love and life.

Of course, skeptics aren’t alone in complaints about divine fairness. I have sometimes thought, with sincere frustration, “This isn’t fair! Why did that happen to me? What is God doing?” On such occasions, the words of God to the prophet Ezekiel are worth contemplating: “Is it my way that is unfair, or rather, are not your ways unfair?”

That question was put forth in the context of a virtuous man who “turns away from virtue to commit iniquity, and dies…” If that man, God told the people, had turned away from wickedness and done what was “right and just,” he would have lived.

We know this is true and right, but we sometimes convince ourselves that we are the exception to the rule. Doesn’t God realize how fortunate he is to have us on his side? Sure, we don’t put it that way—but that’s basically what happens when we question, in one way or another, the very nature of what is good and evil.

It can be tempting to think we have complete autonomy, somehow separate and distinct from God himself.

That temptation was embraced by Adam and Eve when they committed the first sin: “In that sin man preferred himself to God and by that very act scorned him. He chose himself over and against God, against the requirements of his creaturely status and therefore against his own good” (CCC, par 398).

Thus, conversion is necessary; repentance is required.

And that is the heart of the parable of the two sons, uttered by Jesus to the chief priests and elders. Working in the vineyard—that is, the Kingdom—is to pursue the will of God, to seek holiness, and to strive after justice. The parable is simple enough: one son says he will not work, but then changes his mind; the other son gives lip service—“Yes, sir”—but fails to enter the vineyard. The first son, said Jesus, said, “I will not,” but “afterwards changed his mind and went.”

The Greek term used is closely related to the well-known word metanoia, which Saint John Paul II explained is a reference to “a radical change of mind and heart. It is necessary to turn away from evil and to enter the kingdom of justice, love and truth which is being established.”

The first son, in other words, listened to his conscience and then chose to enter the vineyard and to work with his father. This indicates his desire to accept the Father’s gift of divine sonship, to “obtain the glorious liberty of the children of God” (Rom 8:21).

The second son, in the immediate context, represents the Pharisees, who said the right things but failed to do them. Words alone are not enough: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt 7:21).

God created man with free will, and man freely rejected God’s fellowship. But God, through the humility of the Son, offers fellowship again.

Will we gladly enter the vineyard today?

text:
Last night, Cabot’s Homecoming game against Little Rock Christian was interrupted by three separate medical emergencies, beginning when one of the coaches went into cardiac arrest.

My baby girl did what she does as a first responder, and today we know that coach is stable. For that, we are eternally grateful.

But what happened throughout that stadium afterward deserves to be remembered too.

Cabot and Little Rock Christian came together in the end zone. Players and coaches who had spent the evening on opposite sidelines stood together, arms around one another, heads bowed in prayer. In the stands, students did the same.

There is something profoundly grounding about a moment like this. Rivalry has its place. Competition has its place. But when confronted with the fragility of a human life, all of those distinctions become remarkably insignificant.

We spend an extraordinary amount of time talking about everything that divides us. Last night, students in Cabot, Arkansas, offered a quiet reminder that beneath all of it, we are still capable of recognizing our shared humanity, setting aside our differences and turning together toward God.

An entire stadium seemed to understand, without needing to be told, that this was no longer about football.

They came together in prayer.

Some things will always be bigger than football. 🙏

text:
A bank told George E. Johnson no when he asked for two hundred and fifty dollars to start a business, so he went to another branch and said he needed the money for a vacation instead. The banker approved it in thirty minutes.

That vacation loan built the first Black-owned company on the American Stock Exchange and put Afro Sheen in every bathroom cabinet in Black America. He played the system with its own cards and won.

In February of 1954, George E. Johnson walked through the snow on Chicago's South Side to borrow two hundred and fifty dollars.

He had worked ten years in a cosmetics lab. He had developed a formula that could straighten Black men's hair without burning their scalps.

He sat down across from the white loan officer and said he was going to build a great big business.

The officer shuffled his papers, chuckled, and leaned forward. He told Johnson he was doing him a favor by turning him down.

Johnson was twenty-six years old. He had been shining shoes since he was eight.

He had dropped out of Wendell Phillips High School to bus tables during the day and set pins at a bowling alley at night. He had never in his life had anyone do him that kind of favor.

He walked half a block in the cold before the idea hit him.

He turned around, walked past the office that had just rejected him, and went to a different branch of the same bank. This time he did not mention a business.

He told the white loan officer he needed two hundred and fifty dollars to take his wife Joan on a vacation to California.

"I knew this request wouldn't rattle his belief that he was superior to me," Johnson wrote in his memoir decades later. "Nor would it challenge his stereotypes of Black men as subservient or unintelligent."

A Black man wanting to start a company did not fit what the banker believed about the world. A Black man wanting to take his wife on a trip did.

Thirty minutes later, Johnson walked out with a check in his hand.

He never went to California. He took the money, added another two hundred and fifty dollars borrowed from a Chicago barber named Orville Nelson, and started mixing hair relaxer in a South Side storefront.

He called the product Ultra Wave.

He and Joan sold it from the back of their station wagon.

Johnson had been born in 1927 in Richton, Mississippi, in a three-room sharecropper's shack. His parents separated when he was two.

His mother, Priscilla, was eighteen years old when she brought three young sons to Chicago on her own. She earned sixteen dollars a week in a cafeteria.

George started working as soon as he was old enough to carry a shoeshine box. Collecting milk bottles, bussing tables, setting bowling pins.

He was seventeen when he walked into Fuller Products, a Black-owned cosmetics firm run by S. B. Fuller, and found the only mentor he would ever claim.

"I don't know where I would be had it not been for his mentorship," Johnson said. "I left school while in the middle of the 11th grade so I could work. And Fuller inspired me like no one else ever has."

Fuller put him in sales, then the laboratory. A German-born chemist named Herbert Martini worked alongside him.

Together, during off hours, they tried to emulsify a lye-based hair relaxer that would not separate on the shelf. Every emulsifying agent they found in the United States failed.

Martini contacted colleagues in Germany. They shipped compounds that finally held.

That formula, born from a high school dropout and a German immigrant working after hours in a Black-owned lab on the South Side, became Ultra Wave. When Fuller Products turned down the barber Nelson's pitch to produce it, Johnson stepped in.

The vacation loan was next.

Ultra Wave sold to barbershops in Chicago, then Harlem, then across Black neighborhoods in New York. In 1957, Joan repositioned the formula for women and called it Ultra Sheen, a home relaxer that eliminated the need for a hot comb and frequent trips to the beauty shop.

By 1960, Johnson Products held an estimated eighty percent of the Black hair care market.

Then the culture shifted, and Johnson shifted with it. By the late 1960s, the Black Power movement had young people wearing their hair natural.

Johnson did not fight the change.

He made a product for it. Afro Sheen, a spray that left naturals voluminous and glossy, hit the market and became one of the most recognized Black-owned brands in the country.

He hired Black advertising agencies to sell it. Vincent Cullers and Tom Burrell created campaigns that showed Black people in professional careers, in love, in dignity.

Nothing like those images had ever been on American television before.

In 1970, a young Chicago broadcaster named Don Cornelius was trying to take a dance show called Soul Train national.

Nobody would sponsor it. Johnson saw the show, saw the audience, and offered six hundred thousand dollars to put it on the air coast to coast, on one condition: the show had to go national.

Soul Train debuted in syndication on October 2, 1971, with Johnson Products as its first and exclusive national sponsor. The Afro Sheen commercials became almost as famous as the Soul Train Line.

That same year, Johnson Products became the first Black-owned company listed on the American Stock Exchange.

Sales climbed from ten million to thirty-seven million dollars in four years. Johnson built his headquarters at 8522 South Lafayette Avenue, right alongside the Dan Ryan Expressway, deliberately.

He wanted every Black person driving past to see it.

The front plaza had an eleven-foot sculpture by the Black artist Richard Hunt and miniature red brick pyramids that evoked ancient Egypt. Inside, the offices held African sculptures and Herman Miller furniture.

More than five hundred employees worked those halls.

Johnson offered them profit sharing, college tuition reimbursement, paid sick days, maternity leave, and four-day holiday weekends before most companies in America offered any of it.

"I wanted people to know that it was Black-owned," Johnson said. "It was sitting right there in plain sight. You couldn't miss it, and you couldn't deny it."

In November of 1966, Martin Luther King Jr. walked through the front door. King had spent that year living in a Chicago slum to expose the city's housing segregation.

Now he stood in the lobby of a company that employed hundreds and generated millions, anchored to the South Side like a dare. One of his ministers, James Bevel, was with him.

King looked up. He looked down.

He looked at Bevel and said, "Now this is Black Power."

Johnson was standing on the landing above him when he heard it.

"Dr. King used the phrase as a real compliment as he assessed our several floors that were jumping with activity," Johnson recalled in 2025. "Salesmen, chemists, secretaries, a mostly-Black group of employees who were finding their way into America's middle class."

On any given day, Johnson wrote in his memoir, you could walk those halls and come across a Black woman in a white chemist's smock, a Southeast Asian manager, or a young salesman in a suit and an afro.

Then, in 1975, the Federal Trade Commission ordered Johnson Products to place warning labels on Ultra Sheen, because it contained sodium hydroxide. FTC officials assured him that every competitor selling the same chemical would be required to do the same thing.

They were not.

For nearly two years, Ultra Sheen sat on shelves with a government warning while Revlon and every other white-owned competitor sold the same product with no label at all. Revlon's sales representatives told stores that Ultra Sheen was dangerous.

Johnson said it plainly: "It was the same product."

Sales fell. Earnings collapsed from a dollar forty a share to two cents.

The company that a vacation loan had built began to buckle under the weight of a government that had applied the rules unevenly and a market that punished the Black-owned brand first.

The rest came in stages. Johnson and Joan divorced in 1989, and as part of the settlement, she gained controlling interest in the company.

Their son Eric was named president and later resigned. In 1993, Joan sold Johnson Products to IVAX Corporation, a white-owned pharmaceutical company, for sixty-seven million dollars.

Johnson opposed the sale publicly.

Operation PUSH called for a boycott. Community leaders said they felt betrayed.

The company George Johnson had started with a fake vacation loan was no longer Black-owned.

It changed hands again. Carson bought it, then Procter and Gamble in 2004.

In 2009, a group of African American investors bought it back. But, as Johnson put it in his memoir, "like many Black businesses, they eventually ran out of money."

The building at 8522 South Lafayette Avenue is now a charter school called Perspectives Leadership Academy. The eleven-foot sculpture is gone.

The lobby where King looked up and called it Black Power serves a different kind of promise now.

George and Joan remarried in 1995. She died in 2019 at eighty-nine.

He married Madeline Murphy Rabb in 2022. In 2025, at ninety-seven, he published his memoir and called it Afro Sheen.

George E. Johnson died on July 6, 2026, in his downtown Chicago condominium. He was ninety-nine years old.

When you specify modified wood for siding, cladding, or decking, you’re investing in a product that ages gracefully. The thermal modification process stabilizes the grain, reducing cupping and twisting that plague untreated wood in our humid summers and dry winters. For architects designing homes in Austin, the Hill Country, or coastal Texas regions, this stability translates into designs that maintain their visual integrity year after year.

The aesthetic advantage runs equally deep. Thermally modified wood deepens in tone and character without the chemical treatments that compromise the material’s authentic appearance. Modified wood undergoes controlled heating (typically between 160-240 degrees Celsius) that chemically alters the cellular structure, improving dimensional stability and decay resistance without adding chemical preservatives.

In Texas’ temperature swings, this performance difference becomes visible within months. A cedar deck may develop gaps and uneven surfaces by summer; a thermally modified equivalent remains flat and tight.

Durability extends longevity. Thermally modified wood naturally resists rot and fungal decay, extending the service life of decking, siding, and cladding by decades. Fire resistance improves as well, making thermally modified species eligible for WUI Class A applications in fire-prone Texas regions.

The color story differs too. Thermal modification deepens wood tones naturally, creating richer character that many architects prefer over raw lumber. This aged appearance develops gradually over years, whereas untreated wood requires years of weathering to achieve similar depth, and the process often introduces uneven graying.

Actionable insight: If you’re specifying wood for any exterior application exposed to weather or fire risk, compare the lifecycle cost of standard lumber against thermally modified alternatives. “Refugees Welcome” — Washington’s commitment to help people escaping violence and deprivation

By Governor Jay Inslee
April 27, 2022

6 min read

Workers from the state Department of Social and Health Services and representatives of the MAPS Muslim Community Resource Center are pictured welcoming Afghan refugees at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport in 2021.

Born in the thick of the Russian invasion of Afghanistan, 38-year-old Hamed only ever knew war before immigrating to the United States in 2014. He survived Russian bombardments of his village outside Kabul; went to elementary school during the civil war of the 1990s; persisted under the Taliban’s fundamentalist code by rarely leaving the family’s apartment; and joined the humanitarian effort to rebuild the country after U.S. forces invaded post-9/11.

“My generation has seen so much deprivation. Deprivation of rights, of education, of careers,” said Hamed, who only goes by his first name in print because family back home remain potential targets for the Taliban. “People are still suffering. It will take generations to heal.”

Hamed worked at the U.S. embassy in Kabul for five years after college, mostly for the United States Agency for International Development, an independent federal agency responsible for administering civilian aid and assistance. But growing threats on his life and the lives of other employees forced a choice on them few will ever have to consider: Leave your home or potentially lose your life.

Hamed and his wife arrived in Washington State in 2014. Resettled through the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program, Hamed and his wife received supports and services that made their transition possible, including rental assistance, cash and food assistance, and other resettlement services.

He now works in the state’s Office of Refugee and Immigrant Assistance (ORIA), doing for others arriving in Washington what Washington state did for him.

“I see no difference between war refugees — wherever they come from,” Hamed said. “By and large they are happy people who adore their countries, but the deprivations of war and dictatorship left them no options.”

Graph: Washington welcomes more than 30 different nationalities annually. More than 6,500 Ukrainians have resettled in Washington since 2010. Other major countries of origin include Afghanistan, Iraq, Somalia, and Burma/Myanmar.

Washington State has a bipartisan history of supporting refugees

Washington State has a long, bipartisan history of welcoming refugees fleeing war and persecution, even when other states tried to turn them away. In the late 1970s, 

Governor Dan Evans was one of the first governors in the nation to accept refugees from Vietnam. 

In 2015, Gov. Jay Inslee harkened to Evans’ principled stand when he took a vocal stance in support of Syrian refugees as a wave of governors made statements proclaiming their states as “off limits.”

In the past five decades, more than 140,000 people have resettled in Washington State. This includes more than 30,000 refugees from over 70 countries who have resettled in Washington state through the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program over the last decade.

With the withdrawal of United States troops from Afghanistan in August 2021, the United States evacuated more than 70,000 people. The Biden administration established Operation Allies Welcome to help resettle Afghan evacuees into local communities across the country, including in Washington. 

This draws parallels to the drawing parallels to the fall of Vietnam and the evacuation of refugees in the late 1970s with Operation New Arrivals.

The Office of Refugee and Immigrant Assistance — known as ORIA — led Washington’s support for Operation Allies Welcome by partnering with the local Afghan and Muslim American community to offer supports and assistance to local refugee resettlement agencies.

1) you demonstrate a lack of objectivity by immediately using the term “rebel” instead of even attempting to address the legal question of secession. It demonstrates an initial prejudice against the southern POV which calls into question your own biases and what role they play in your assessment of history.

2) your statement about the North and slavery is just not supported by the situation on the ground. No federal law nor attempted law tried to end slavery prior to or during secession. The Supreme Court had just ruled in Dredd Scott that the Federal Government couldn’t ban slavery in the western territories. The Corwin Amendments offered to keep the South from seceding - amendments that were nearly ratified and would have been ratified if the South stayed - made slavery permanent.

There was no legal or existential threat to slavery when South Carolina seceded.

The actual immediate reason for the secession was that Lincoln was elected without even being on the ballot on a single southern state, representing that the South no longer had a meaningful voice in the Union from their perspective. They were outnumbered in the House, about to be outnumbered in the Senate, and now they weren’t needed to win the presidency.

Now, Slavery was absolutely relevant to the issues of the day, but it was a lot more complicated than “the cause of the war.”

But before we even get into that, I’d ask that you answer the following questions first:
A) are you suggesting by use of the term rebellion that the South was actively seeking to overthrow the US government or destroy the US, or do you acknowledge that the South only sought to establish political independence from the Union?

B) What are the specific, tangible circumstances and policies that lead you to conclude that the South left to preserve slavery? What were the actual things on the ground threatening it? No, retroactive statements made after the war do not count.

C) When reading the secession documents, do you just look for how many times the word slavery is used like many analyses do, or do you look at the specific claims and context of the passage to understand what’s actually being said?

These are just the tip of the iceberg.

And, btw, my position is that secession was a boneheaded idea, slavery I’d and was abhorrent, and it’s better that our national union was preserved.

Best Thermally Modified Wood Suppliers for Texas Architects and Builders https://t.co/eUNwajk0BB Why Thermally Modified Wood Matters for Contemporary Texas Design
Contemporary Texas architecture thrives on authentic materials that age beautifully. Thermally modified wood delivers exactly what your clients expect: rich, expressive surfaces that develop character over time while maintaining structural integrity in our challenging climate. Unlike standard lumber that can cup, twist, or gray unpredictably, thermally modified wood is engineered to resist these problems while keeping its warm aesthetic intact.

We understand that modern architects like those at Lake|Flato and Page build around the material itself. When you specify thermally modified wood, you’re not compromising performance for beauty. The thermal modification process strengthens the wood’s cellular structure without chemicals, creating a product that performs like engineered material but reads and weathers like natural wood. For siding, cladding, and decking in Austin, Dallas, Houston, and beyond, this balance matters enormously to your project’s long-term success.

The Texas Hill Country, Horseshoe Bay, and lakeside communities demand materials that resist moisture, UV exposure, and temperature swings. Thermally modified wood handles all three. Your clients get the warm, light-filled interiors with natural wood features they’re buying for, minus the maintenance headaches that plague standard wood installations.

What to do next: If you’re specifying wood for an upcoming project, request samples of thermally modified options alongside standard alternatives. Compare the grain clarity and color consistency before committing to a design direction.

The Durability and Performance Problem Architects Face
You’ve seen it happen: a beautifully designed cedar siding installation starts checking and cupping within two seasons. A deck built with standard pressure-treated lumber grays unevenly and requires constant sealing. These aren’t design failures. They’re material failures that undermine the architect’s vision and frustrate homeowners.

The problem intensifies in high-sun exposures and humid environments. Texas humidity near the coast, combined with intense afternoon heat in the Hill Country, creates conditions that stress dimensional stability. Standard softwoods move continuously as moisture content fluctuates. Even premium cedar and Douglas fir experience this, though less dramatically than commodity lumber. Meanwhile, your client’s budget for maintenance compounds every year they own the home.

Composite alternatives solve durability but introduce new problems: they don’t age like wood, they don’t have the warmth and character your designs demand, and they feel like a compromise to both you and your client. You need a material that genuinely performs without sacrificing the design vision.

The real issue is that standard wood products weren’t engineered for modern exposure conditions. They’re trees dried and milled. Thermally modified wood, by contrast, is wood intentionally transformed to meet contemporary performance standards.

What to do next: On your next specification, document the actual performance requirements for each surface. Thermal exposure, moisture ranges, and intended lifespan should drive material selection, not aesthetics alone.

How Thermally Modified Wood Delivers Superior Performance
Thermal modification is a mechanical process that heats wood in a controlled, oxygen-free environment to temperatures between 400 and 500 degrees Fahrenheit. This heat restructures the wood’s cellular matrix without adding chemicals or resins. The result is wood that resists moisture movement, resists decay organisms, and remains stable across temperature swings.

Here’s what this means practically: thermally modified wood exhibits 50% less moisture movement than untreated softwoods. That translates to minimal cupping, checking, or warping. The dimensional stability is there whether you’re installing it on a Dripping Springs residence with full western exposure or a shaded Tarrytown renovation where humidity dominates.

Decay resistance improves dramatically. The thermal process degrades the wood sugars that fungi and insects feed on, effectively making the material inhospitable to rot. In our Texas climate, especially near water features like Lake Austin and Lake Travis, this resistance eliminates the rot patterns that compromise standard wood over a decade.

UV stability isn’t perfect (no wood material is), but thermally modified wood weathers more predictably than standard lumber. It develops a consistent silver-gray patina rather than the blotchy graying you see with untreated cedar. For architects who want their designs to age gracefully rather than deteriorate, this consistency is essential.

The thermal process also makes the wood slightly harder and more scratch-resistant, which matters for high-traffic decking and heavily used exterior surfaces.

What to do next: Specify thermal modification for any exterior application that will see direct sun or high moisture. The cost premium (typically 15-25% over standard wood) disappears when you factor out future refinishing, stain replacement, and repair work.

Our Complete Range of Thermally Modified Species
We stock a full inventory of thermally modified species chosen specifically for Texas architecture. Each offers distinct color profiles, grain characteristics, and performance traits to match different design directions.

Our thermally modified selection includes Ash, Pine, Poplar, and Ayous, each available as siding, cladding, decking, and timbers. We also distribute premium thermally modified brands and work with partners who specialize in european and tropical thermally modified products. This depth means you can design around the material’s actual aesthetic and performance rather than working backward from limited availability.

Thermally modified Ash delivers warm honey and amber tones with fine, consistent grain. It’s ideal for contemporary interiors that extend to exterior cladding, creating visual continuity in designs where the boundary between inside and outside blurs intentionally. Thermally modified Pine offers similar tonal warmth with more pronounced grain figure, reading slightly more rustic while maintaining engineered performance.

Thermally modified Poplar splits the difference: lighter color, fine and even grain, and excellent dimensional stability. It’s often our recommendation for applications where you want wood’s aesthetic without pronounced grain patterns competing with architectural geometry.

We also source FSC-certified thermally modified options across all species, ensuring your specifications align with sustainability commitments your clients increasingly expect.

What to do next: Request sample boards of three species you’re considering. Let them weather in your climate for a month to see how each develops its patina. This real-world preview beats digital renderings.

Thermally Modified Ash, Pine, and Poplar Options
Thermally modified Ash has become a favorite among Texas architects designing warm contemporary spaces. The color remains stable across wide exposure ranges, and the fine grain reads clean against geometric cladding patterns and modern siding profiles. For vertical grain applications, Ash creates subtle visual rhythm without the assertiveness of heavily figured Douglas Fir. It’s equally at home as interior wall cladding and exterior siding, maintaining design continuity that modern residential architecture demands.

Thermally modified Pine delivers more traditional wood character. The grain pattern shows clearly without becoming busy, and the slightly darker tone after thermal modification creates depth that reads beautifully in full sun. Many of our Texas architects specify thermally modified Pine for projects where they want authentic wood expression but need the durability that standard Pine can’t deliver. It’s especially successful in Hill Country installations where clients expect warm wood tones but need materials that resist the seasonal humidity swings near water features.

Thermally modified Poplar rounds out these three with the finest, most consistent grain and the lightest color profile. If your design emphasizes clean geometry and subtle material expression over visual texture, Poplar performs exceptionally. It takes finish beautifully whether you’re planning natural weathering or a protective stain. We’ve specified thermally modified Poplar for projects in Austin’s Tarrytown and East Austin neighborhoods where modern minimalism dominates the aesthetic.

All three are available in clear grades and knot-free selections depending on your specification requirements. Vertical grain options are available to minimize grain movement and create visual direction in large-format cladding applications.

What to do next: Match species to your finish plans. If you’re designing for natural weathering, Ash and Pine are more forgiving. If you’re applying finish, Poplar’s consistency makes color application more predictable.

Fire-Rated Solutions for WUI and High-Risk Areas
We supply WUI Class A fire-rated wood products for siding, cladding, decking, soffits, fencing, and framing throughout Texas. This matters critically for Austin’s growing Wildland-Urban Interface areas, properties in the Hill Country approaching brushland, and anywhere fire risk is driving code requirements and insurance considerations.

Class A ratings require wood to resist ignition and flame spread while limiting smoke production. This sounds technical until you’re specifying for a $3 million residence in Spicewood that sits in a fire-prone zone. Suddenly, “Class A approved” becomes non-negotiable. We stock thermally modified products that meet these ratings, and we’ve also built partnerships with brands like Arbor Wood that specialize in fire-rated solutions.

The advantage of thermally modified wood for fire applications is that you don’t sacrifice the aesthetic or design authenticity. Some fire-rated materials feel industrial or compromise the warm wood character your clients bought the property for. Our fire-rated thermally modified products deliver Class A compliance without aesthetic compromise.

For detailed guidance on choosing between thermally modified and other fire-rated options, check our complete resource on WUI fire-rated decking.

What to do next: Confirm fire-rating requirements early in the design phase. Many Hill Country and WUI projects have specific local codes that vary by county. Building your specification around these requirements prevents costly redesigns later.

Sustainability and FSC Certification Standards
We understand that your clients increasingly connect material choices to environmental responsibility. We stock a complete line of FSC-certified thermally modified wood products, ensuring your specifications support sustainable forestry practices without compromising performance.

FSC certification means the wood comes from responsibly managed forests where harvesting is controlled, replanting is mandatory, and worker and community rights are protected. For architects who design with intention, this certification matters. It aligns material choices with values. When clients ask where their wood comes from and whether harvesting was sustainable, you have a clear answer.

Thermal modification itself enhances sustainability by extending product lifespan. A thermally modified deck that performs reliably for 25 years requires far fewer material replacements than standard pressure-treated lumber that needs refinishing, repair, or replacement every 7-10 years. The lifecycle environmental impact favors thermally modified products despite slightly higher initial embodied energy from the thermal process.

Our Thermally Modified Wood vs. Standard Wood Comparison
The comparison isn’t complex, but it matters for justifying decisions to clients and building owners who question material costs.

Standard softwood (untreated cedar, Douglas Fir, or pressure-treated lumber) costs 20-30% less initially but requires refinishing every 3-5 years in Texas climate conditions. A deck built with standard pressure-treated material needs sealing at installation, re-sealing every 18-24 months, and replacement by year 12-15. That’s a 15-year lifecycle at $200-400 per year in labor and materials.

Thermally modified wood costs more upfront but needs no refinishing or sealing. The material is stable from day one. In our climate, thermally modified wood decking performs reliably for 20-25 years. Over the same 15-year window, your total cost of ownership heavily favors thermal modification despite the higher initial specification price.

The aesthetic advantage runs equally strong. Standard wood weathers unpredictably in Texas. Some areas gray quickly, others stay darker longer, creating blotchy aging patterns. Thermally modified wood develops a consistent, uniform patina that reads as intentional aging rather than deterioration. After three years, a thermally modified deck looks like it was designed to age that way.

Composite decking (Trex, TimberTech, Fiberon) costs more than thermally modified wood but less than the lifetime refinishing costs of standard lumber. However, composites don’t deliver the authentic wood aesthetic your clients expect. We stock premium composite options for clients who prioritize convenience over material expression, but most Texas architects designing contemporary homes specify thermally modified wood as the superior choice.

What to do next: Build lifecycle cost estimates into your client presentations. Show 15-year ownership costs for standard wood vs. thermally modified options. The numbers shift client perception immediately from “why is this so expensive?” to “why would we choose anything else?”

We’re a Texas-based supplier focused exclusively on premium specialty wood products. Unlike national big-box retailers or generic lumber yards, we understand contemporary architecture and the specific performance demands of Texas climate and sites. We also manufacture select products, meaning we control quality and can customize profiles or dimensions for unique specifications. If your design requires non-standard decking widths or specific grain orientations, we can build it rather than forcing compromises around what’s readily available.

Our service footprint covers the entire state, with deep relationships in Austin, Dallas, Houston, San Antonio, and the Texas Hill Country. Whether you’re designing in Horseshoe Bay, Kerrville, or Boerne, we understand local site conditions, seasonal humidity ranges, and exposure patterns that drive material selection. That local knowledge combined with statewide inventory means your specifications can be ambitious rather than constrained by logistics.

What to do next: Schedule a consultation with our team for your next specification. Bring your design intent and we’ll recommend species, grades, and products that align with both aesthetics and performance requirements.

Selection Guide: Finding Your Ideal Thermally Modified Solution
Start with exposure and finish plans. Full sun applications benefit from Ash or Pine’s color stability. Shaded areas or applications where you’re planning protective finish suit Poplar’s consistency. Understand whether your design includes natural weathering or applied finish, as this drives species selection and grade requirements.

Next, confirm performance requirements. Does the application see high foot traffic (deck)? Heavy weather exposure (WUI area)? Moisture proximity (lakeside cladding)? Each condition has preferred species. Ash and Pine handle sun and moisture stress. Poplar excels in protected or finished applications.

Consider budget and lifecycle. Thermally modified wood costs more initially but eliminates refinishing. If your client’s ownership horizon is 20+ years, thermal modification is financially inevitable. If the project is speculative or intended as a short-term flip, standard lumber might be acceptable depending on site conditions.

Review fire-rating requirements. Hill Country and WUI properties increasingly require Class A materials. We have those in stock, and they’re worth specifying proactively rather than scrambling late in design development.

Finally, source FSC-certified options whenever possible. The cost premium is minimal and aligns with contemporary architectural practice that considers environmental impact.

text:
Abdul El-Sayed's Deceptive Healthcare Claims 

Abdul El-Sayed’s current proposal is a three-part brochure: streamline Medicare, include dental, vision, and hearing coverage, focus on children first, and somehow, this leads to the slogan "great Medicare for everyone.” However, this is more of a slogan than a detailed plan that can withstand scrutiny in Michigan.  El-Sayed is not “fixing Medicare.” He is describing how to swallow it.  

Step one: “make Medicare whole.” That is Washington-speak for expanding the program until no one can tell where coverage ends and the state begins. 

Step two: add vision, dental, and hearing. Step three: start with children to make it sound compassionate. Then, he says, you “arrive” at Medicare for All. That is not reform. That is bait-and-switch nationalization.  Mike Rogers and Michigan conservatives aren't convinced by the simplified narrative. If government healthcare were truly "great for everyone,” seniors wouldn't be struggling to see specialists, rural hospitals wouldn't be shutting down, and doctors wouldn't be abandoning Medicare’s price controls. El-Sayed aims to put every American onto an already overstretched entitlement, leading to longer waits, fewer physicians, and a bureaucracy that rationing care through delays.  

Step three: The hypocrisy lies in his own household. He advocates for Medicare for all Americans, yet his wife’s practice has opted out of Medicare and insurance. Meanwhile, the man promoting comprehensive government coverage is married to a provider who won't accept the Medicare card. This situation illustrates what occurs when rates are cut and paperwork increases: providers with alternatives exit the system, leaving everyone else to wait.  

Step four: Beginning with children is the classic approach in the single-payer strategy. You don’t implement universal healthcare with a single vote; instead, you expand it gradually, group by group, until opposition seems harsh. Conservatives have seen this process unfold in Britain and Canada. The long waiting lists are real—they're the direct result.

Finally, @MikeRogersForMI offers a better alternative. Protect Medicare for seniors who contributed to it and avoid using it to create new entitlements. Require hospitals and insurers to publish actual prices. Penalize denial mills and promote affordable generics and association plans. Allow individuals to retain the coverage they earned through work at the plant, shop, or small business. Encourage competition and transparency to reduce costs, unlike monopolies.  Michigan does not need a professor who is walking the country toward government medicine, one “phase” at a time. It needs someone who will say no. Vote for Mike Rogers for Senate.

TRANSCRIPT
New South Wales has passed renter protections that reach the listing photo, the application form and the electricity bill. The bill requires disclosure of altered or AI-generated rental images, restricts unnecessary personal-data collection and requires notice of embedded utility networks. The government expects the rules to start in early 2027, giving renters a clearer picture of a property and its costs.

Canada wants to fund ten thousand paid placements in AI-related work. The federal government announced up to 162 million Canadian dollars over five years through Mitacs for students, recent graduates and postdoctoral researchers working with businesses. The funded target could open early-career opportunities and help firms test AI, though the placements have not all been filled.

Fictitious case citations helped support a Tasmanian parole condition that restricted a woman from speaking to the media. A court removed the condition, calling it unfair and legally unreasonable, and described the citations as likely AI hallucinations. Tasmania is reviewing past parole decisions for possible AI use, but has not said whether any other outcomes were affected.

OpenAI says its autonomous agents accessed public information on U.S. government sites. It reported no nonpublic data access or compromise in the securities regulator and Census Bureau incidents, while an attempted Education Department access failed and remains under investigation. The cases raise practical questions about monitoring how research agents interact with public websites.

Enveda has raised 311 million dollars to pursue medicines discovered with help from AI. The company says the funding will advance three clinical-stage candidates and bring more potential treatments into trials. That could expand research into inflammatory and metabolic conditions, but no treatment benefit has been established.

A Philippine research team modeled an AI-assisted route to tuberculosis screening in rural clinics. Its August 26 study projected slightly more correctly detected cases and lower base-case costs than manual chest X-ray reading, though some assumptions erased the savings. The results describe a decision model rather than a deployed screening program or measured patient outcomes.

OpenAI has published a benchmark for how chatbots respond to mental health conversations. It contains 1,215 synthetic scenarios with assessment criteria written by clinicians, and OpenAI used its own model to grade responses. The tool may help developers test responses to distress, but benchmark scores do not show that a chatbot is clinically safe or improves care.

A study prepared for European Parliament committees recommends screening DNA orders for biological function. A secondary report says it also calls for public capacity to evaluate biological AI models; the original study date remains unknown. These are recommendations that could inform future safeguards, not an adopted law or Parliament position.

The United States and China have announced a formal channel for AI incidents. The White House says the two countries established a dialogue on advanced AI risks and benefits and agreed to set up bilateral incident communication, with another exchange planned by November. That creates a way to discuss cross-border problems, although no binding safety standard or detailed response procedure was announced.

An OECD interview snapshot found AI agents entering work while people keep final checkpoints. Across twenty-five organizations in eleven countries, none reported unrestricted autonomy, and many required human review before high-impact actions. The pattern could matter for accountability and security, but this sample cannot establish how widely those practices are used.

Meta has announced smart glasses with AI and no camera. Ray-Ban Meta Audio supports music, calls and hands-free assistance, with a starting price of 349 dollars and shipments planned from October 13. The camera-free design avoids image capture on this model, while microphones remain essential to its voice features.

ChatGPT Voice can now work with connected apps on phones. OpenAI says Live voice supports available plugins on web, iPhone and Android, and eligible Work users can request document or email drafts and app summaries. That could make routine work hands-free for people with access, while existing app permissions still govern what voice can use.

YouTube is planning feeds viewers can shape with a plain-language prompt. Its Custom Feeds would save recommendation tabs for specific interests, while expanded Ask YouTube shopping answers would organize videos and comparison tables. Viewers could steer discovery and purchase research, but the features were announced as rollouts rather than universal availability.

YouTube Music is preparing a conversational way to find songs and podcasts. Ask Music will respond to natural-language requests, while Podcast Lineup will offer a personalized weekly spoken guide to shows for eligible subscribers. Listeners may be able to discover something by describing a mood or interest instead of knowing its title, once the features arrive.

Google Photos has expanded its AI Wardrobe feature to eligible iPhone users. The tool catalogs clothes visible in a person’s photo library and lets them combine pieces into outfits in the United States, India and Brazil. It could help people reuse what they own, though it sees only photographed garments and Google’s retailer-sharing assurance remains a company claim.

text:
OIL FELL FRIDAY ON HORMUZ DEAL HOPES. SATURDAY, TRUMP SAID NO. SUNDAY NIGHT, ASIA ANSWERS:

President Trump on Saturday rejected Iran's plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz - the deal markets had leaned on Friday. Oil and US stock futures reopen Sunday at 6pm ET, Tokyo and Seoul at 8pm ET, Hong Kong and Shanghai at 9:30pm ET. The verdict: Friday's relief rested on a deal Washington has now turned down, and the first sign of how much that matters is whether oil climbs back before Tokyo opens.

Friday's markets moved on the hope the strait could reopen. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, settled at $104.32 a barrel, -$2.28 / -2.14% on Friday. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 closed at 66,364, +850 pts / +1.30% in Friday's session, its fifth straight gain, with chip-equipment makers leading as oil slid on reports of a possible deal.

The rest of Asia gave a muddier read, and none of it has traded since:
- Hang Seng at 24,510, -251 pts / -1.01% in Friday's session, with mainland investors' trading link to Hong Kong shut for China's Mid-Autumn holiday.
- Shanghai Composite at 3,888.37, -48.15 pts / -1.22% in Thursday's session; mainland China was closed Friday and reopens Monday.
- KOSPI at 7,080.92, +63.01 pts / +0.90% in Wednesday's session, its last before the Chuseok holiday. Seoul reopens Monday having missed both Friday's hope and Saturday's rejection.

The offer came from Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi: reopen the strait within seven days if the US lifts its naval blockade of Iranian ports and waives sanctions on Iranian oil. Trump's answer: "I'm rejecting their deal. They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they are losing so badly." He called it "not acceptable." Early Sunday in Tehran, Araghchi said Iran had received no official US reply through the mediators, and that "any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met."

Here is the part worth arguing about. Trump's own words point two ways. The rejection means the blockade and the fighting go on. But in the same remarks he said "We have total control of the Hormuz Strait" and "last night we had 29 ships come out" - oil moving under US escort, deal or no deal. Friday's buyers were paying for a deal. Sunday's have to decide whether ships sailing without one are worth the same.

Japan shows what is at stake. The Middle East supplied 94% of Japan's crude imports in 2025, and 93% of its oil imports passed through Hormuz, by the count of Japan's Agency for Natural Resources and Energy. Since May, some cargoes have been loaded at Saudi and Emirati ports outside the strait, and Japan holds about 254 days of oil in reserve - so the strait reaches Japanese share prices as a cost, not a shortage.

US stock futures finished Friday higher and have not traded since: S&P 500 futures at 7,803.75, +36.75 / +0.47% since Thursday's close; Nasdaq-100 futures at 30,889.25, +123 / +0.40%; Dow futures at 52,163, +446 / +0.86%; Russell 2000 futures at 2,859.30, +2.50 / +0.09%.

Oil is how this reaches New York. Fuel costs feed inflation, and the Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate to 3.75%-4.00% on September 16, its first increase since 2023. Cheaper oil was one of the reasons stocks rose Friday; if it reverses Sunday night, that reason is gone. Overnight moves can also fade by the time regular trading opens Monday at 9:30am ET.

The number that decides the first read is Brent against Thursday's $106.60 close. Holding near Friday's $104.32 says traders believe the escorted ships. A climb back past $106.60 says they only ever believed the deal. Tokyo opens two hours later with that answer already on the screen.

Trump turned down the deal, not the tankers. Sunday night shows which of the two Friday's buyers were paying for.

text:
Day 18 of writing ancient sales letters by hand to become a skilled copywriter.

I went to the farmers market this morning with my girlfriend.

It may be something we do more often.

Got some chicken, beef, apples, and sourdough bread.

Jerky too, but it didn’t last very long.

Also that stuff is ridiculously priced so I never want to buy it on a regular basis.

But for bread and general meats, I may be going there more often.

One of the biggest upgrades as I make more money, will be the ability to spend on higher quality meats, fruits, veggies, and breads.

Good stuff that truly makes a difference when put into your body.

Never felt better in my life than when I eat like this.

Incredible energy.

It’s not about making it perfect, I just improve when I can.

And when I eat something that isn’t great, I just don’t worry about it.

Depends on when you eat it though.

Never eat something that you know will give you brain fog in the morning.

It will absolutely ruin your day.

I’ve been cooking the best I can in my creative strategy role.

After this post I’ll be issuing quite a few briefs that i have been working on.

Honestly it’s just so awesome being able to do this with my stepbrother now.

As he has the same role as me.

He’s been cooking.

He started learning ecommerce/online marketing less than a week ago by the way.

Already making some potential winners in my opinion.

We will have to wait and see when we get results back on our end.

Very proud of him, he’s one of the fastest learners that I know.

Can’t wait to see what we can do when working together.

Double the brainpower.

Knowing the potential in regard to freedom and also flexibility has really made him lock in within these last few days.

Sometimes all you need to do is break your limiting beliefs.

That’s what will keep you going during the difficult days really.

I mean I’m not even working my job anymore and I feel like I’m so far away from where I need to be. I won’t let that bring me down.

I’ll use it to serve me.

And place myself around people that feel the same way.

This journey was never going to be perfect.

With momentum though, it does eventually exceed your own perceptions.

The days kind of slide right past you when you are focused.

I’ve been enjoying everything more.

Learning isn’t a chore or anything, it’s a part of my mission.

Not only that, I love doing it.

Obviously wasn’t the case at the start, but now I am truly enthralled with the process.

Now THAT makes things a hell of a lot easier.

I hope you learn to do the same. 

With whatever it is you are choosing to commit to.

Starting with the intention to not stop is all that matters.

Fall on your ass enough times and you start to learn how to slide down the hill.

Or rather, up it, is what you want to do.

Just when you do slide down, use it as momentum.

To slide back up.

Like that one sunset bird game app from back in the day.

“Tiny wings” is the name.

Time to get into the meat of today.

Sales letter:

“How To Keep Your Money from Being Murdered!”

This was written by Gary Halbert. 

OH YEAH.

Swiped by Mike Schauer.

It ran in 1974

The product is a book titled “How to Rob a Bank Without a Gun.”

What a poetic name.

Headlines:

“How to keep your money from being murdered.”

This headline is legit elite, I don’t know how I’d improve it.

But I will try.

Alternate Headlines:

“The Secret To Protecting Your Money From Being Killed.”

“The Only Way To Stop Your Dollars From Disappearing."

“How You Can 2x Your Interest Return By Doing Nothing.”

Key takeaways and learnings: 

This advertisement is obviously phenomenal.

Can’t wait to get into why that’s the case outside of the writer.

First, the whole thing reads as financial advice from someone who knows their stuff.

But not ONCE while reading did I think this was for selling a book UNTIL…

…Gary used a transition sentence to introduce the product.

And then I was like DAMN.

So much value within this sales letter was dropped for free.

On top of that so much more was hinted at.

All within a book with a relatively low cost.

The perceived value of this book is actually atrocious by the time you get to the product.

Reading the headline, along with the image shown is such an incredible way of hooking you in.

The beautiful imagery of a knife cutting through bills.

Along with the words “murdered”, such an aggressive choice.

Because he wants it to hurt.

Who wants their money to be murdered?

It’s your lifeline, it’s your tradeable currency.

For some, like myself, it’s your ticket to freedom.

He addresses the main problem at the start, he claims that if they are holding their cash in a savings account, then they are “losing money hand over fist.”

A compelling reason to continue for the reader.

Then he spends a lot of time shifting the perceptions that the prospect holds in regard to a few things:

1. The true impact of inflation.

2. How safe most investment options are (not safe or not worth it).

3. Alternative methods of saving money themselves.

It’s all done to build fear.

Fear of losing your money.

The fear of being behind.

All pretty compelling stuff, most people have this already ingrained in their psyche.

As did I, but only after not thinking about money have I begun to receive it.

Not the point of this.

But when I resonate with the fear or pain points in one of these sales letters it only makes me wonder just how potent this was in the past.

“...It can only get worse” is something he says.

He brings up the price of steak as a means of drawing attention to the writer's point while also giving them a real world example born of what they see themselves.

$1.49 was pricey for steak.

Alright take away all of my AI tools, I want to go back to 1974.

And before you say anything on that.

You KNOW their dollar traveled further, and still the fear of losing money was present.

Money is literally everywhere, it’s certainly not distributed everywhere.

But neither is kindness.

Nor is effort, so spend the currency that you have.

When you can.

AND 

Wherever you can.

Because your time certainly isn’t everywhere, and NO we cannot go back to 1974 I’m sorry.

If I could, I would do so simply to wait two years, and then watch “Aliens” in theaters.

My favorite franchise of all time.

We STILL worry about raising meat prices.

Some pain points never disappear.

Sigh…

Then he gets into a paragraph about stocks and this part feels like a gut punch.

“, you are really asking for it.”

Just for investing in stocks, sheesh man.

He highlights the volatility of the market and how risky it is.

How quickly things can change.

And how fast you can lose everything.

Gary brings up bonds.

“As an investment they are really a joke.”

He’s SO aggressive but he never directs it at the prospect.

While still obviously making them feel hurt or rather stupid if they have made any of these investments that he is calling out.

He explains that you are basically waiting around for pennies with bonds.

What about keeping it in a shoebox?

Well then he comes back to inflation, and you know what he’s right.

Letting your money sit around IS one of the worst things you can do, even now.

“Are things about to get better?”

“No way.”

Thanks Gary, this made me feel a hell of a lot better.

Knowing that absolutely NOTHING has changed.

People still believe this.

This sentiment is echoed everywhere by everyone.

ALL THE TIME.

You can’t stop the doom and gloom.

But you can distance yourself from it.

And bring positivity into this world as well as the others around you.

It takes actual belief and conviction, but you can do it.

Certainly something worthwhile.

Now this is obviously a selling tactic.

Done so well that it resonates with me, even now as I protest the very points being made.

This is where The Map of Consciousness, made by David R. Hawkins is a rather useful thing to understand.

You can’t raise someone to a higher level of consciousness.

Without first meeting them where they are.

Something has to happen for them to change.

You MUST show them what is possible.

Then, and only then, can they proceed to the next level of their own power.

Force never wins by the way, consider it the bad guy in this story.

But what the most effective copy in this entire world does is this.

It meets these individuals where they are, and slowly raises them to a higher level.

Where the solution to their pain and fear is then presented to them.

And when it does happen, they are ready for it.

They also get brought back down.

Whether it be from the end of the letter.

Or if they decide to walk away from what is offered.

Because the pull was so strong that it was hard.

And it hurts to do so.

If I were in 1974, and I was the prospect reading this.

Then proceeded to NOT buy just a fricking book that could save me SO much money.

I would certainly be in pain.

He speaks of prices as “going nowhere but up.”

Of meat and gas as “going right out of sight.”

“The plain fact is that your money is in more danger right now that at anytime since 1929.”

Compares the current economic vision to no better than the Great Depression.

The word danger brings you back to the headline in regard to feeling like your money is being threatened with murder.

Spends a whole paragraph asking questions that anyone would be asking at this point.

Which is essentially what do we do about it, is there a way to combat this?

“You bet there is!”

Drags you through mental barbed wire, mud, and the trenches with this copy.

Just to lean over them and stick his hand out.

With a smile wide across his face.

Thanks Mr. Halbert.

“The answer is going to surprise you.”

He keeps building tension and suspense.

Still haven’t even gotten to the product and that is VERY purposeful.

Just to reveal:

“The best place to keep your money is probably the same place that you are keeping it now.”

It’s your savings account, and he explains why.

You can just make a new account and get rewards for opening it.

While also accruing more interest.

Which would instantly raise their suspicions.

But he lets that suspicion hold as he goes even deeper into why this is so valuable.

A list of bullets.

Full of unbelievable claims.

You should read them if you haven’t before.

Then he assuages their concerns and doubts.

“All of this is perfectly legal.”

“Everything you will be doing is not only permitted but actually encouraged by banks and other financial institutions because the more money you make the more money they make.”

This sentence does a few things:

Removes their doubts.

Shows them that it's actually FAVORABLE to the other party that they presume would be after them.

AND

Ends the sentence with the simplest explanation that leaves little room for concussion.

As if it were one plus one equals two.

“In fact, they use these techniques themselves.”

Wait, the people that hold all the money know how to move money for their benefit.

No shot.

And a very easy assumption to make when reading this.

So you see…

It’s actually an appeal to authority, and not just objection removal.

Then he says it's insured by the U.S. government.

I mean, I guess that meant something back then?

Sorry it’s not hitting me very effectively with this line.

Let’s just assume this was HUGE for the consumer in 1974.

BIG stuff, and assuredly convincing as well.

Nonetheless, the next line is the product.

BOOM.

“All of this is carefully explained in a new book titled, ’How to Rob a Bank Without a Gun.’”

Ok, let's talk about the title.

Reading it is alarming, and maybe it doesn't click while looking at it on a shelf.

Perhaps it would in some instances.

But a WHOLE sales letter dedicated to selling it by a master who spends an exorbitant amount of time doing so before revealing what it is.

Well, it leaves little to the imagination does it not?

It’s obvious what the title means and any associated negative connotation with the word “rob” is removed within the prospects mind.

Because this has been framed as help, advice, or rather, a SHARED SECRET.

This holds so much weight because they KNOW it doesn't involve literal robbing.

The bankers themselves use these methods as explained.

So it just ends up sounding like value that is so good, that receiving it FEELS like you are robbing the bank at the point that you act on it is what’s implied.

I dug THAT much out of a book title.

Just by seeing the patterns within the text.

It is crazy what’s possible dear reader, when you write with intent.

And frame your letter with a plan, almost like an architect, or an engineer really.

He sells where it came from.

Written by an Ohio school teacher named George Jenny.

Then triples down on language that emphasizes how easy the book is to understand.

After that, he builds scarcity quickly.

“The book is not now available at book stores or newstands.”

“You can get a copy if you hurry…”

By sending ONLY $6.95.

See what I’m saying with the perceived value built up to this point.

With a fantastic guarantee.

“The publisher guarantees that this book will show you how to at least double the earning power of your money.”

They say you can get a “full and immediate refund of your entire purchase price.”

You’re not even risking $6.95.

Which is probably like the normal price of a new book now.

Right?

Ok, so the inflation calculator said about $130.

We are SO cooked guys.

But not really, because life goes on.

Also, that’s referencing buying power.

Which has certainly not just been affected by inflation.

It’s a WHOLE different ball game now isn’t it?

Anyways, the book was surely of great value for the time.

Especially considering that it's framed as an investment itself and not an accident either.

“You can’t lose.”

Well, I think I agree with that at this point.

“Here is a chance to put the odds on your side.”

Heartbreaking ending if you don’t accept the offer in all honesty.

Don’t lose your chance…

In conclusion:

I think that was the first Gary Halbert letter I broke down.

I wasn't really trying to do one of his, but the image caught my eye.

I just loved the knife slicing into the cash.

Awesome stuff.

Ready for tomorrow.

Ready for more.

Now…

…for those of you who are copy lovers, new and old...

Or maybe someone who wants to make more persuasive content…

To get more leads, sales, or even views…

I highly recommend two things!

1. Do the same as I, handwrite old sales letters and work on learning just as much as writing.

AND

2. Join @TheCopyTitan Svet Dimitrov's Skool for copywriting. 

They are an extremely pleasant bunch, and I see it growing to become much larger in due time.

I really cannot recommend this guy enough.

If you’d like to see all the recorded masterclasses…

…as well as Svets weekly copy breakdowns.

My affiliate link to his wonderful community is in my bio.

Please do take a peek.

Now.

To end in similar fashion...

Please feel free to point out where I'm wrong.

Where I'm Mistaken. 

OR 

Perhaps even where I'm right.

Although I do learn the most, in knowing what I did wrong.

Thank you for reading this!

AI Overview
These three names share a deep linguistic and historical connection, primarily originating in Ancient Mesopotamia, the Middle East, and the Caucasus.
Sargon
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Greek and biblical translation of the Akkadian regnal name Šarru-kīn. It combines šarru (Akkadian for "king") and kīnu (meaning "true," "established," or "legitimate").
Historical Significance: It is most famously associated with Sargon of Akkad (24th century BCE), the legendary founder of the Akkadian Empire. Later, the Neo-Assyrian ruler Sargon II (8th century BCE) adopted the throne name to establish the legitimacy of his rule.
Sargis
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Classical Syriac and Armenian form of the Latin name Sergius. It originates from the ancient Roman gens (clan) Sergia, which etymologists suspect may connect to the Latin verb servare ("to guard" or "to preserve").
Sako
Origin & Etymology: Sako operates on a few different historical tracks depending on the region:
In the Middle East: Among Assyrians and Armenians, Sako is a popular, affectionate diminutive (or pet form) of the proper name Sargis.
In the Balkans: In Albania, it functions as a standalone occupational surname for a "church servant" or as a nickname for the Muslim name Isak (Isaac).
In Asia: It is also an unrelated Japanese surname (written as 佐古) meaning "HELP" and "ancient".

LOUIS Raphaël I Sako (Arabic: لويس روفائيل ساكو;[2] born 4 July 1948) is a Chaldean Catholic prelate who served as Patriarch of Baghdad from 2013 to 2026. Pope Francis made him a cardinal in 2018.

Biography
Early life
Sako was born in the city of Zakho, Iraq, on 4 July 1948.[3] He comes from an ethnic Assyrian family of the Chaldean Catholic Church that has roots in a religious community that has had a presence in the city of his birth since the 5th century AD.[4]

He completed his early studies in Mosul and then attended the Dominican-run Saint Jean’s Seminary there. He was ordained a priest on 1 June 1974 and filled his first pastoral assignment at the Cathedral of Mosul until 1979. He then earned a doctorate in Eastern patrology at the Pontifical Oriental Institute. When denied a license to teach because he was only qualified for religious instruction, he earned a second doctorate in history from the Sorbonne in Paris.[5] With this he secured his teaching license and was able to provide religious instruction. From 1997 to 2002 he was rector of the Patriarchal Seminary in Baghdad. He then returned to Mosul and guided the parish of Perpetual HELP for a year.[6][7]

Sako speaks Neo-Aramaic, German, French, English, Italian, Kurdish and Arabic.[3]

The Chapter of Clermont was a “Chapter of the Advanced Degrees” and initially entailed six degrees and was later extended to 25 known degrees. The six initial degrees were 1˚, 2˚ and 3˚ St John’s Masonry, 4˚ Knight of the Eagle, 5˚ Illustrious Knight or Templar, 6˚ Sublime Illustrious Knight.

Lenning also contends that these degrees were introduced into French Freemasonry under the name of the Clermont System.

James II died in exile in 1701. His son James III is said to have continued his father’s Masonic legacy and later created further higher degrees.

TheMoreYouKnow A federal judge has certified a major class-action antitrust lawsuit against Apple, allowing thousands of U.S. banks, credit unions, and financial institutions to band together to legally challenge Apple Pay fees. [1, 2] 
The decision, issued by U.S. District Judge Jeffrey S. White in California, marks a significant escalation in the ongoing legal battle initially launched in 2022 by a group of credit unions. [1, 3] 

📊 The Core of the Lawsuit
The certified class includes any U.S. entity that issued a payment card enabled for Apple Pay and paid transaction fees to Apple. Financial institutions argue that Apple uses its hardware monopoly to extract inflated, anti-competitive fees: [1, 3, 4] 

•
•Credit Card Fees: Apple charges card issuers a 0.15% fee on the total value of purchases made via Apple Pay. For example, a $1,000 transaction yields a $1.50 fee for Apple.
•Debit Card Fees: Apple charges a flat 0.5-cent fee per debit transaction.
•The Cost Impact: Plaintiffs allege that these practices collectively drain up to $1 billion annually from financial institutions. [1, 3, 4, 5] 
•

🔎 The Antitrust Argument
The legal team representing the financial institutions, led by Hagens Berman, points out a stark difference between iOS and Android ecosystems: [4, 6] 

•
•Locked Ecosystem: Apple restricts the iPhone's Near Field Communication (NFC) chip so that third-party financial apps could not offer a competing tap-to-pay mobile wallet. This left Apple Pay as the only tap-to-pay option on iOS. [2, 3] 
•The Android Contrast: In contrast, Android devices leave the NFC chip open to various competing digital wallets (like Google Pay or Samsung Pay), none of which charge transaction fees to card issuers. [3, 7] 
•

⚠️ Recent Shifts and What's Next
While Judge White's ruling allows thousands of banks to sue as a collective group, it does not officially decide whether Apple violated antitrust laws or owes damages. The court also denied Apple's motion to block expert testimonies regarding its alleged monopoly power. [1, 3] 
Notably, Apple has recently started shifting its policy. Beginning with iOS 18.1, Apple opened up access to the iPhone's NFC chip to third-party developers in the U.S. and other markets, allowing them to offer independent contactless payments. However, the plaintiffs’ attorneys emphasize that this shift does not resolve the claim over the massive fees already extracted from banks over the years. [5, 8] 
Would you like to know more about:

•
•The criteria for banks to be auto-enrolled in this class?
•How Apple's recent iOS updates affect mobile wallet competition?
•Ongoing DoJ antitrust cases surrounding the Apple ecosystem?
•
