Japan and South Korea Take Contrasting Paths to Attracting Chip Plants—but Share a Government–Industry Disconnect

Satoru Oyama’s Industry Scope (104)

Published September 18, 2026, at 11:00 a.m. | Satoru Oyama (Grossberg), EE Times Japan

I attended a forum in Gwangju, South Korea, a city seeking to attract semiconductor plants. Yet neither Samsung Electronics nor SK hynix—the companies it hopes to bring in—was represented. Their absence suggested a gap between the government’s enthusiasm and the companies’ own positions. Japan and South Korea face contrasting circumstances in the semiconductor industry, but both have a disconnect between government and business. Their experiences show why semiconductor strategies must take account of what companies actually need and intend to do.

On September 10, 2026, I was invited to speak at a Semiconductor and AI Forum in Gwangju. The South Korean government and local authorities are committing substantial funding to a flagship initiative to build a semiconductor and AI hub there. Put plainly, they want to attract memory-chip plants from Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, South Korea’s two leading semiconductor companies.

The organizers apparently thought Japan’s success in bringing a TSMC plant to Kumamoto might offer a useful model, which is why they invited a Japanese speaker like me. To state my conclusion up front, however, I worry that the Gwangju initiative will be extremely difficult to carry through. What I saw at the forum offers a way to examine South Korea’s situation alongside Japan’s efforts to attract semiconductor plants.

No one from Samsung or SK hynix attended

I find it hard to imagine the Gwangju initiative succeeding without the support of Samsung and SK hynix. They are the companies the city is trying to attract and the central players in the proposal. If both wholeheartedly backed building plants in Gwangju, the project would likely proceed smoothly. Yet neither company sent anyone to the forum, despite its sizable attendance of about 140 to 150 people.

Of course, their absence does not mean they oppose the plan. They may simply have been unable to attend. Even so, they could have passed a message to the lawmaker or the local mayor who gave keynote speeches stressing the importance of the initiative—something along the lines of “We have high hopes for this project” or “We are considering it with a view to building a plant.” Unfortunately, no such message was presented. At the very least, the two companies do not appear to be embracing the project wholeheartedly.

This was my first time attending a forum or similar event in South Korea. Frankly, I do not know what is customary there or precisely how this event differed from others. Still, the forum’s scale, the positions held by its keynote speakers, and the sight of everyone standing with their right hands over the left side of their chests to sing the national anthem all conveyed an extraordinary sense of commitment. I could feel how strongly those involved wanted to succeed and turn Gwangju into a major semiconductor and AI hub. If that is the goal, surely winning the support of the two companies should be the first priority.

South Korea needs another semiconductor hub

Investment in South Korea’s semiconductor industry is extremely active, but its existing hubs in Yongin and Pyeongtaek face growing constraints. These include shortages of land, pressure on power and water infrastructure, and an increasingly crowded supplier base. That creates a need to spread major new investments beyond the area around Seoul.

Gwangju, in southwestern South Korea, is one candidate. Since 2020, the government has also been developing it as a leading AI city. In other words, Gwangju already has an AI foundation that could make it easier to build an integrated semiconductor and AI cluster.

Development in Gwangju extends beyond those two fields. The city is being prepared as a proving ground for future industries, including a next-generation automotive industrial park, autonomous-driving systems, smart energy and green technology. The government sees strong links between these industries and semiconductors and AI, and has taken a highly proactive stance toward the region.

A gap between government and industry

The South Korean government, eager to advance the Gwangju initiative, has already announced plans described as “₩800 trillion of investment in the southwest” and “two new sites in Gwangju for Samsung and SK hynix.” But these are the government’s plans; the two companies have not agreed to them. My candid impression from the forum was that their attitude toward the project is cool.

For example, speakers repeatedly emphasized their hopes for the future, but said nothing about support for the two companies they hope to attract. I am not suggesting that the government has decided against providing such support. Still, should it not have explained what benefits the project would offer Samsung and SK hynix? How will the people driving the initiative make their case to two companies that did not attend the forum? If my reading of the situation is right, a strategy to win over those companies is what the project needs most.

Where Japan and South Korea differ—and where they are alike

As noted at the outset, I was asked to attend the forum to discuss examples of government-led efforts to attract semiconductor investment in Japan. I spoke about TSMC in Kumamoto and Rapidus in Chitose, Hokkaido.

Before turning to those cases, I made a point of saying that Japan and South Korea are in different positions. Japan regards semiconductors as an important industry, but its domestic companies alone do not have enough momentum to deliver the expansion the government wants. It has therefore committed large subsidies to attract a foreign company, TSMC, and helped establish a government-led company, Rapidus. South Korea, by contrast, has two major companies actively expanding their businesses under their own power. I recommended that its government first establish what those companies want and what kind of support would actually help them.

The contrast is striking: in Japan, the government is eager to build a semiconductor industry while the private sector is relatively cautious; in South Korea, private companies are aggressively expanding their semiconductor businesses while the government pursues a strategy of its own. What the two countries share is a mismatch between government and business.

Private companies are the main drivers of economic activity. But because the semiconductor industry directly affects national strategy and economic security in every country, governments also become involved, each side approaching it from its own position. Their priorities often diverge.

As someone who works in the semiconductor industry, I envy the energy of South Korea’s companies. At the same time, I find it frustrating: since that energy already exists, why not understand what the two companies want and find a way to build on it? Watching the forum, I even wondered whether those promoting the project hoped to draw on the companies’ strength without taking their wishes into account.

Japan, meanwhile, adopted a semiconductor strategy in 2021. It noted that the value of domestic semiconductor production had remained around ¥5 trillion from 2011 through 2020 and set a target of ¥15 trillion by 2030. Kioxia’s recent advances may help put the industry on an upward trajectory, but they will not be enough on their own to reach ¥15 trillion. Construction has begun on TSMC’s second Kumamoto plant, yet the target remains demanding. Nor can Japan count on a substantial contribution from Rapidus by 2030.

I would argue that meeting the target requires an increase in domestic DRAM production. That raises two possibilities: attracting one of South Korea’s major chipmakers or persuading Kioxia to enter the DRAM business.

Several media outlets have recently reported that SK hynix might accept an invitation from Miyagi Prefecture. I have to say I find those reports highly questionable. Miyagi had originally prepared to attract Taiwan’s PSMC, but those talks unfortunately fell through. The suggestion now seems to be that it could pursue SK hynix instead. Yet the requirements for PSMC’s proposed medium-scale production of legacy logic chips and for SK hynix’s large-scale production of leading-edge DRAM, including HBM, are entirely different.

A large leading-edge DRAM plant, for instance, raises the question of whether to install five or ten EUV lithography systems, each requiring more than one megawatt of power. That question would never arise in the same way for medium-scale legacy logic production. Is it responsible to circulate rumors that “perhaps SK hynix will come” while overlooking such fundamental differences? Semiconductor demand driven by the AI boom is concentrated in leading-edge logic and memory. Attracting companies that make those products requires serious preparation and commitment from the host region, as well as from the companies themselves.

Governments need to work more closely with industry

I mentioned the possibility of Kioxia entering the DRAM business because I believe it is at least plausible. Many people with DRAM experience remain at the company; the field is not entirely unfamiliar to it. But Kioxia is unlikely to decide on its own to start a DRAM business. The risks and costs would be substantial. This is precisely where government support is needed.

The Takaichi administration has put forward targets for domestic semiconductor production—¥15 trillion in 2030 and ¥40 trillion in 2040—but listing figures is hardly a strategy. Why did Japan’s semiconductor industry decline in the first place? How could production actually reach ¥15 trillion or ¥40 trillion? Whether those targets are achievable depends on the strength of private companies. Unless the government better understands the realities they face, setting targets alone will accomplish little. As things stand, the gap between government and industry will only widen.

What support, for example, could the government provide if Kioxia were to establish a DRAM business? If that is not feasible, what strategy could persuade one of South Korea’s two major chipmakers to manufacture DRAM in Japan? At the very least, Japan might have a chance if it developed an offer more attuned to what those companies want than Gwangju’s appears to be.

In both Japan and South Korea, governments will struggle to put their policies into practice unless they pay much closer attention to the companies involved. Attending the forum brought that home to me once again.

text:
If you missed it

Calls / non-calls that reasonably smell
1.  Vonnahme 21-yarder (early 4th, set up 14-13) Shoved out, came back, caught a tipped ball. Legal only if it was a true force-out and he re-established before the catch. A teammate tip does not make him eligible again. Replay left it. That is the “exception for the offense” play.
2.  No 10-second runoff at 0:02 First down in bounds + Michigan player down + two seconds left. That is the exact runoff situation. Michigan should have been able to take 10 seconds and end it. Reporting that Iowa “declined” the runoff is backwards administration if Michigan never got the choice.
3.  Injury timeout as a free reset Same play. Iowa could not spike under three seconds. Daley going down stopped the clock and let them line up a designed fade instead of a panic heave. Even if the injury was real, combining it with a skipped runoff is what makes it look like a gifted extra play.
4.  Iowa false start ~0:28, no runoff talk Clock was running in the last minute. A false start that prevents the snap is a classic 10-second-runoff foul if the clock was moving. Iowa had already used its last timeout. If officials treated the clock as already stopped, no runoff; if it was running, Michigan should have been offered 10 seconds there too.

2.  No 10-second runoff at 0:02 First down in bounds + Michigan player down + two seconds left. That is the exact runoff situation. Michigan should have been able to take 10 seconds and end it. Reporting that Iowa “declined” the runoff is backwards administration if Michigan never got the choice.
3.  Injury timeout as a free reset Same play. Iowa could not spike under three seconds. Daley going down stopped the clock and let them line up a designed fade instead of a panic heave. Even if the injury was real, combining it with a skipped runoff is what makes it look like a gifted extra play.

Iowa had already used its last timeout. If officials treated the clock as already stopped, no runoff; if it was running, Michigan should have been offered 10 seconds there too.

text:
Thank you @revanth_anumula garu.

 A Heartfelt Tribute to Dr. Manmohan Singh

Today, as I stand and reflect on my life journey, I cannot separate my story from the story of India's economic transformation.

I was born in 1986 into a remote tribal family living in extreme poverty. My parents struggled to raise nine children. We lived in a small hut, often uncertain about our next meal. Food was scarce, and rice was a luxury for us. Many nights, I cried for rice. Our family survived mainly on ragi, wheat, millets, roots, and forest produce. I still remember how my younger uncle would save a plate of rice for me every night and morning because he knew how much I longed for it.

Those were difficult days. Poverty was not a statistic for us. It was a daily reality.

Yet, through government schools, tribal welfare hostels, educational opportunities, and the expanding aspirations of a changing India, my life slowly transformed. My brother and I joined a tribal Ashram school. Education opened a door that poverty could not close. Step by step, that journey eventually led me to the Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati.

When I look back, I see more than my personal struggle. I see the impact of policies that empowered millions of ordinary Indians. I see the vision of leaders who believed that even the poorest child in the remotest village deserved an opportunity.

Among those leaders, Dr. Manmohan Singh occupies a special place.

At a critical moment in India's history, when the nation faced a grave economic crisis, Dr. Manmohan Singh helped lay the foundation for a stronger, more resilient, and self-confident India. Through wisdom, integrity, and economic foresight, he contributed to opening new opportunities for generations of Indians. His work helped create an environment where talent, regardless of birthplace or background, could aspire to something greater.

For people like me, his contributions are not merely economic reforms. They are stories of hope. They are stories of children who moved from huts to universities, from poverty to possibility, from survival to dignity.

I remain deeply grateful to the vision and contributions of leaders such as Jawaharlal Nehru, Indira Gandhi, Rajiv Gandhi, P. V. Narasimha Rao, and especially Dr. Manmohan Singh, whose leadership helped shape modern India's economic architecture.

The statue of Dr. Manmohan Singh in Hyderabad is not just a monument of stone and metal. It is a symbol of gratitude. It represents the dreams of millions of Indians whose lives were transformed by opportunity. It honors a statesman of remarkable humility, a distinguished scholar, an economist of global stature, and a leader who believed in the power of knowledge, hard work, and inclusive progress.

For millions of families who rose from poverty, Dr. Manmohan Singh's legacy lives not only in economic data or policy documents, but in our homes, our education, our aspirations, and our achievements.

As someone who once cried for a plate of rice and later walked the halls of IIT Guwahati, I offer my deepest respect and gratitude.

Thank you, Dr. Manmohan Singh. Your legacy is written not merely in history books, but in the lives of millions of Indians who dared to dream and were given a chance to succeed.

text:
Add two quiet layers that deepen the rite without extra ritual: 

Sit for a few minutes after the offering and recall one specific story or quality of a grandparent or parent, .Pitru Paksha 2026 is underway (roughly 26–27 September to 10 October, ending on Sarva Pitru Amavasya). The original post already lists sound traditional practices. These refinements keep the same spirit while making them more complete, consistent, and personally meaningful.

Face south after bathing, take a brief sankalpa (your name, gotra if known, and the ancestors you intend to honour), then offer water mixed with black sesame through the pitru-tirtha (the space between thumb and index finger). Repeat for three generations on both paternal and maternal sides, or simply “all ancestors of this line” if names are lost. Do this daily even on non-matching tithis; the specific death tithi or 10 October remains the strongest day.Prepare a small sattvic meal (kheer, rice, or simple vegetables without onion/garlic), set a portion aside before you eat, and offer it with the same intention used in Tarpan. Feed crows, a cow, or a needy person afterward. If you cannot make pindas, donate uncooked grains or a cooked meal in the ancestors’ names—the intent transfers the merit. Keep the home quiet and avoid meat and alcohol throughout the fortnight
And, if possible, involve younger family members so the lineage memory continues. On 10 October perform the fuller version (Tarpan plus charity) for everyone whose exact tithi you missed. 

Consult your family elders or a trusted priest for any regional or gotra-specific details

text:
#PITRU_PAKSHA:

Pitru Paksha is very important 16 days  (सोलह श्राद्ध)  

What should you do during Pitru Paksha?   Pitru Paksha is not merely a period of rituals.   It is a sacred time to remember our ancestors, express gratitude towards them, and pray for their peace and liberation.  

Here are some traditional practices.  
1 Feed a crow In Hindu tradition, the crow is associated with the ancestors.   It is believed that our ancestors can symbolically receive food through the crow.  Therefore, feeding a crow during Pitru Paksha is considered auspicious.  

2 Perform Tarpan on their Tithi If you know the tithi on which your ancestor passed away, perform Tarpan on that day by offering water mixed with black sesame seeds in their name.  

3 Donate according to your capacity You may donate sweets, clothes, food, or fodder for cows.   Even a simple act of feeding a crow or a needy person can be done with the intention of remembering your ancestors.  

4 Keep your home Sattvic Traditionally, meat and alcohol are avoided during Pitru Paksha.   Keep the atmosphere peaceful and spend time remembering your Ishta Devata or Kul Devata.  

5 Maintain purity while performing Tarpan Take a bath and perform Tarpan with cleanliness, devotion and a calm mind.   Before eating, you may keep aside a small portion of food as an offering for your ancestors. 

 6 Chant a Pitru Mantra You can chant.  

ॐ पितृभ्यः स्वधायिभ्यः स्वधा नमः। ॐ पितामहेभ्यः स्वधायिभ्यः स्वधा नमः। ॐ प्रपितामहेभ्यः स्वधायिभ्यः स्वधा नमः।  

Om Pitrubhyah Swadhayibhyah Swadha Namah Om Pitamahebhyaḥ Swadhayibhyah Swadha Namah Om Prapitamahebhyaḥ Swadhayibhyah Swadha Namah 

 This is a traditional way of offering reverence to the ancestors.  

What if you don't know your ancestor's Tithi?  You can perform Pind Daan and Tarpan on Sarva Pitru Amavasya, which is traditionally dedicated to honouring all ancestors.  

Pitru Paksha reminds us that we are not disconnected individuals we are part of a lineage.  

Remembering our ancestors is a way of expressing gratitude for the lives, sacrifices and blessings that came before us.  

May our ancestors attain peace and liberation.

  ॐ पितृभ्यः स्वधा नमः।

I never thought I’d depend on college placements. For me, placement was always the last option - “If nothing works out, I’ll get placed through college anyway.”

But after seeing what’s happening with my friends, even that doesn’t feel like a great backup anymore.

Because honestly, if someone gets a ₹20–30k/month job in a Tier 1 city with a 2-year agreement, how are they supposed to survive for those 2 years?

If you’re in your 1st or 2nd year at a Tier 3/4 college, please don’t be completely dependent on college placements.

Pick a skill. Try different things. Build projects. Get internships. Freelance. Make connections.

Just make sure that by 4th year, you have enough skills and options that you don’t NEED your college to get you a job.

text:
3 days of whirlwind pilgrimage across Varanasi and Ayodhya.

Maybe it was a case of bigotry of low expectations, but was pleasantly shocked by how clean and well-maintained both cities were. Varanasi, especially.

Even around the temple in Kashi (teeming with people and buzzing with commercial chaos), rarely encountered a garbage dump, an overflowing sewer or the kind of pervasive filth type sterotypes . Rest of the city was as good as what an tier 2 Indian city can offer. 

The city (at least place close to the hotel we stayed) even had kind of continous pedesterian paths that allowed me a good morning walk  Frankly, it was a striking departure from the visual reality we encounter in some of India’s most prosperous cities, including Mumbai and Bengaluru.

Ayodhya–Faizabad is still very much a work in progress. But besides the magnificent temple ( the newly minted temple aesthetics who criticise are such a joke), what struck me was the transformation underway. The donations controversy hurt many who had given in good faith, yet the faithful seems to have stayed steady.

Never took any of the famed 9-10 expressways of UP. Yet the 300–400 km or so that we travelled on NH and state roads were, in many stretches, comparable to what one encounters in Tamil Nadu or south/central Karnataka. 

The rural landscape too looked remarkably familiar. children flocking to schools, two-wheelers filling the roads, plenty of good wayside hotels and greenery everywhere. There was remarkably little visible evidence of the kind of stark poverty one often associates with the these parat og Hindi heartland.

Didn't converse on politics (my Hindi isn't up to it), but a few locals (cab driver, guide, shopkeepers) did, unprompted and with real pride in how much the region has changed. Many credited both the PM and the CM. 

Of course these are surface impressions, UP is an extraordinarily complex  and large state, with social and caste dynamics no road trip can decode. Plus dont understand politics very deeply like 'strategists' and journalists. But the scale of visible change is hard to dismiss, and it will be surprising if it doesnt shape the politics that follow.

Sixteen hours of no food. That is Rogan’s whole protocol.

Elon offered the other half: eat the good stuff, just less of it. Rogan runs a stopwatch. Water and coffee until the window opens. He says the weight stays when he keeps it and comes back when he doesn’t. Not a temple. A kitchen with hours.

What the fasting window can do, if you actually eat less overall: fewer mindless calories, an easier time dropping weight, a break from all-day insulin spikes for some people, and a simpler rule than counting every gram. It is not a cure. Sleep, protein, and what you eat when the window opens still decide if this is useful or just a late breakfast with branding.

text:
I appreciate your sincerity and the exposition. You've taken some time with the motive to defend your beliefs while reaching out. I have responded in kind and though lengthy I hope you'll read all. God bless.
I agree with most points of your explanations, but there are several reasons to be concerned about the level of veneration afforded Mary by the RCC as well as other things
One example, consider referring to Mary as "Mother of God" as opposed to the more concise "mother of Jesus". They justify this because Jesus is God. But why would God be pleased with this: which God? Though it's understood to be Jesus by Christians, "Hail Mary, Mother of God" is uttered and written countless times every day around the world, often in public.
But "Jesus" is the name above all names and there is no other name under heaven whereby men must be saved. Every knee shall bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord to the glory of God the Father.  "Hail Mary, Mother of God" puts the emphasis on Mary, not Jesus, leading to inappropriate veneration of Mary at the expense of the name of Jesus. Many unbelieving hearers will think Mary is at God's level.
Outside of the gospels, Mary is hardly mentioned and Paul never mentions her by name. The apostles and disciples had one focus: spreading the Gospel of Jesus Christ in faith and in the power of the Holy Spirit.
If the RC position was correct, the surely the dogma would have been alluded to in the writings of Paul and the other apostles. Instead, there was no focus on Mary.
Catholic dogma venerating Mary such as the immaculate conception, her perpetual sinless virginity and her assumption certainly do not have much scriptural support, which is at best ambiguous if not contradictory.
For example, many had pointed to Luke 1:28, "And the angel (Gabriel) being come in, said unto her: Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women" to say that Mary was always filled with grace and thus without sin. Prolonged debate eventually led to the acceptance of the IC as dogma in 1854.
Why is it so important for Mary to be sinless (free from original sin)?  From the RCC perspective if she wasn't then her perpetual virginity and assumption immediately come into question, but basically it's the belief that God would not have Mary as a fleshly temple if she was impure. 
But Christ himself took on the form of sinful flesh and God would later indwell sinful men, adopting them as his children through the Spirit of adoption, the Holy Spirit, as it says in Gal 4:6
"Because you are his sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, the Spirit who calls out, “Abba, Father.” So there was no need for Mary to be sinless since Jesus was sent to save and indwell sinners."
As blessed as Mary was, God's graciousness to her as sinner in need of a Savior, brings greater glory to God than declaring her "sinless". The IC is neither needed nor has the necessary robust scriptural support nor was a foundational tenet of the apostles and the early church.
Rather, as stated in Romans 5:12, the apostle Paul writes: "Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned" If you are not born of God, then you're a sinner in need of salvation. Those born of God have received the Holy Spirit, "be baptized and receive the Holy Spirit." 
The Assumption of Mary is even more scripturally fanciful than the IC, and was not accepted as dogma until 1950 and I won't address that. But the perpetual virginity of Mary requires speculation wrt several problematic verses: Mathew 1:25 "But he did not consummate their marriage until she gave birth to a son. And he gave him the name Jesus." "Consummate" has the obvious meaning. And Mathew 13:55 “Isn’t this the carpenter’s son? Isn’t his mother’s name Mary, and aren’t his brothers James, Joseph, Simon and Judas?" and there are other sibling references. I've explained why the IC is not very persuasive and unnecessary and it makes more sense to accept that Mary had children. Catholics simply accept the edicts of the Church as a duty but for those who are not RC, there is no reason to believe their dogma wrt Mary. The appeal to the authority of the Church based on their faith in the veracity & purity of apostolic succession and often call sincere questioners "heretics".
Though Christians can appreciate and honor Mary in their hearts, the problem is that honor and worship can become conflated in practice, and sometimes in the heart. Gabriel did not kneel before Mary and whenever men kneeled before angels or men, they were rebuked because kneeling was considered an act of worship reserved for God. “When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshipped him. But Peter lifted him up, saying, ‘Stand up; I too am a man’” (Acts 10:25–26). Kneeling before men in connection to reverence to God is totally unacceptable and, however  pure your intentions, building statues of Mary and kneeling before them is even more unacceptable. The trend of the RCC over the centuries has been towards an increasing veneration of Mary. The apostles Peter and Paul would never have let this practice develop or continue.
There is good reason for those of us who are not Catholics to question an unbroken chain of apostolic succession. I won't go into them except to note its current state and a bit of history. The early church, at least up until the Constantine, reflected the love, humility and power of Christ through the Holy Spirit. Jesus had no place to lay his head and the apostles, the leaders of the church, and others, were persecuted as the offscouring of the earth and martyred. Christians often met in houses and had things in common and great grace was upon them and were also persecuted, but the gospel spread effectively with Christ as the head, giving guidance through the Holy Spirit. 
The current church bears little resemblance: very rich and making a great show of it, much more political, formal, exclusive and tightly controlled, no great demonstration of the power of the Spirit. 
The sins of the RCC are many. The Crusades, the atrocities of the Inquisition, treatment of native populations, sexual scandals, etc. This is not to diminish good work done, or the sincerity and sacrifices of many Catholics throughout history, but only to point out this behavior points to the fact that political/spiritual corruption entered in, and this affected the operation of the church and necessarily its judgements regarding dogma and the evolution of their practice. There's no reason to believe Peter & Paul would be pleased with the current state of the RCC and there's no reason to simply accept RCC dogma based on the claim of apostolic succession without question.
Regarding baptism and the new birth:
All those baptized by John for remission of sins had not received the Holy Spirit since the Spirit was not given until after Christ's resurrection (on the Day of Pentecost). So although baptism prepares the body to receive the Spirit, it's important to make this distinction. The act of God in sending the Spirit into your heart as the Gift of Christ, follows the act of faith of the believer of repentance and baptism. Although baptism accompanies salvation, salvation of the spirit and the new birth result from the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, joining your spirit to the Holy Spirit, resurrecting your spirit in Christ so you can walk in newness of life. As it says in 2 Cor. 17-18 “Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new. And all things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ, and hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation.”  Your identity is now in and of Christ.
And Paul declared in Gal. 2:20 "I have been crucified with Christ and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me. The life I now live in the body, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me."
The indwelling of Christ makes us holy children of our Father, but now by faith, just as we received him we are to continue in him (looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith) so that Christ lives in us, and through us, so that being God's workmanship in Christ Jesus both the fruits of the Spirit and accompanying works are manifested as being wrought in God and that the excellency of the power is of God, not men.
To properly understand the relationship between faith and works as it relates to the indwelling of Christ (the new birth) go back to the OT.
The eternal Abrahamic Covenant was established based on his one act of obedience of faith in offering up his son Isaac, the seed of promise, believing God could raise him from the dead. And this was accounted as righteousness apart from the works of the law (not yet given). 
The one act of obedience on our part bringing salvation is to repent believe the gospel, "be baptized and receive the Holy Spirit" This faith justifies us because it's faith in the one act of obedience of Christ: his eternal sacrifice. And the New Covenant in HIs Blood now applies to believers, and we are accounted righteous because of faith apart from works, just as Abraham was. Just as death entered into all through Adam's one act of disobedience (no fault of ours), now justification and eternal life are offered to all freely (no credit to us) through faith in Christ's sacrifice and the indwelling of the Holy Spirit. We are justified by faith apart from any works resulting from our ongoing obedience to Christ and the Holy Spirit working in us to will and do his pleasure. Romans 10 makes this perfectly clear.
There's much more that could be said but if you've made it this far then it's more than expected.

text:
27 September 2026
Today in History

1652
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Daybreak brought a cloudy day at the Cape.
It rained from time to time during the day.

1653
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
The rain from the previous day continued.
Nobody complained, however, as the rain was beneficial to the crops.
It did not rain continuously, and the men were therefore able to sow several seedbeds.
The diary also mentions that the whales were constantly blowing and frolicking in the bay.
The Commander writes that it was pleasant at times to stop work for a moment and watch them playing and thrashing their tails.

Sunday, 27 September 1654
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Morning brought a cloudy day with a light southwesterly breeze.
A ship, the Gidion, left Table Bay during the morning and continued her voyage.

1655
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Daybreak at the Cape, as on the preceding two days, was pleasantly cool and cloudy.
The wind was moderate and continued to blow from the northwest.

1656
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
The south-southeasterly wind, as on the preceding two days, continued to blow without let-up.
A soldier, Pieter Matthijsen, belonging to the ship Princes Roijael, died during the morning.
The cases of two sailors, Jan Leendertssen and Jan Meijns, were heard that day.
Both men came from the Princes Roijael.
Officers from the Roijael, as well as from the Zeeridder and the Emlo, served as the presiding officials.
Both men were accused of attempted arson and incitement to mutiny.

1657
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Dawn at the Cape broke pleasantly and without incident.
The wind was moderate and blew from the northwest.
Work began that day on supplying the Rotterdam with provisions.

1658
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Daybreak is described as cloudy, with rain from time to time.
The wind was moderate and blew from the south-southeast.
Chaihantima, a captain of the Chainouqya, arrived at the fort during the day with 14 cattle and 21 sheep.
The transactions were concluded to everyone's satisfaction.

1659
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
The day is described, as on the previous day, as cloudy with rain from time to time.
During the morning the Commander held a meeting with the officers of the Erasmus, which was anchored off the fort.
The major question was whether the Erasmus could safely resume her voyage back to the Netherlands.
The officers agreed that extensive repairs would have to be undertaken.
The repairs were estimated to take approximately three months.
In the meantime, the Erasmus would be supplied every second day with a sheep, vegetables, and other provisions as required.
Fifteen sailors would come ashore to assist wherever help was needed.
The latter would be regularly rotated so that everyone could, as the saying goes, “stretch their legs” for a while.

1666
Cornelius van Quaelbergen was appointed Commissioner at the Cape in place of Zacharias Wagenaer.

1830
Hendrina Johanna Susanna Joubert (née Botha)
Hendrina Johanna Susanna Joubert, born Botha, was born at Richmond, Cape Colony.
Hendrina was a child of the Great Trek and experienced both the hardships and joys of the Trek at first hand.
Hendrina personally experienced the battles of Vegkop (1836) and later Veglaer, which lasted for three days in August 1838.
Her brother, Joachim Botha, was one of the three scouts sent out shortly before the Battle of Vegkop to reconnoitre the Matabele.
Joachim was also one of those who were murdered together with Retief at Umgungundlovu.
After the British occupation of Natal, she and her parents left the area and settled at Potchefstroom.
It was at Potchefstroom that “Drienie,” as she was sometimes known, met Piet Joubert, the future Commandant-General of the South African Republic.
Ten children were born from their marriage.
Something of her character can be seen in the fact that, before the First War of Independence, she transported a load of rifles to her husband in an ox-wagon.
The significance of the incident is perhaps best appreciated by the fact that she undertook the task together with her young son and simply did what had to be done.
According to tradition, she was also the person who first spotted the “Redcoats” on the mountain shortly before the Battle of Majuba.
Taking the above into consideration, it is clear that she regularly accompanied her husband to the battlefield.
Drienie was also at the forefront on 4 August 1915, when approximately 5,000 women marched to the Union Buildings to plead for the rebels of the 1914 Rebellion.
From there the women proceeded to Church Square, where, among other things, Psalm 146 was sung.
This remarkable “Mother of the Nation” died during September 1916.
The newspaper De Volkstem wrote of her:
“She was a woman without fear or reproach — the darling of a nation.”

1835
The recollections of the Voortrekker J.H. Hatting during the Great Trek.

1839
Andries Pretorius was not the type of man who could easily be caught napping during the day.
When Panda sent word that he and his entire following were on their way to Pietermaritzburg, Pretorius raised a commando and rode out to meet him.
Pretorius had Panda and his people halt some distance away and sent Hans “Dons” de Lange ahead to deliver a message to Panda.
In short, the message was that Panda should leave his followers behind and come forward together with his captains so that they could talk.
In the end, the asylum Panda had requested was granted to him and his people.
Panda and his people were given a piece of land on which to live.
They were to settle there under the direct supervision of Hans Dons de Lange.
Out of gratitude, Panda presented the commando with 80 oxen.

Tuesday, 27 September 1836
From the diary of Louis Tregardt.
Gustav came on horseback to visit his parents.
Carolus worked on the water furrow during the day.
Another two cattle died.
According to an entry later in October of the same year, Carolus intended to build a dam.
He was, however, unsuccessful time and again and eventually abandoned the attempt.

Wednesday, 27 September 1837
From the diary of Louis Tregardt.
(The following entries in Tregardt's diary are particularly long and extend over almost three full typed pages.)
As usual, the party was ready to trek at daybreak.
When the oxen were brought forward, Louis noticed that an ox was missing.
Louis realised that something was wrong, since an ox and five cattle had also disappeared the previous day.
He immediately had his horse saddled, took his panga gun and rode out towards the cattle.
Jan's horse was already saddled and he rode with Louis.
When they reached the cattle, Louis and Jan counted the animals and found that another five were missing.
In other words, they were now short of ten cattle and two oxen, and one can understand why Louis was angry.
Louis and Jan soon returned to the wagons.
When they arrived, Louis asked one of the local people of colour to take him to the local chief.
Jan rode with him once again.
Louis and Jan were received by the chief.
The man, however, knew nothing about the missing animals and offered to help search for them.
After the interview, Jan and the guide returned to the encampment alone.
Louis decided to go to their former campsite to see whether the cattle might perhaps be there, or whether they had possibly fallen into a trapping pit.
Louis was still some distance from the old camp when he saw vultures circling in the light.
When he reached the spot, he saw that one of the missing oxen had fallen into a trapping pit and that some of the local people had speared the animal to death.
Louis was, to put it mildly, unimpressed.
He was about to turn his horse around and return to the encampment when he noticed several local people.
When he asked who had speared the ox, he was pointed towards a nearby kraal.
By that time, however, the sun was already beginning to set, and Louis realised that he would have to reach the encampment.
Louis was still on his way when he suddenly found himself in the midst of an entire series of trapping pits spread across a large area.
He pulled the horse back, but it was too late and the horse fell into a pit.
(The reader should have no illusions about these trapping pits. Most of them were “armed” with sharpened stakes, so that an animal would often suffer a cruel death upon impact.)
Louis realised that he was in serious trouble and that the sun was going down.
He could not free the horse and therefore walked to a nearby kraal.
On arrival, he first had to find the entrance.
The moment he entered the kraal and began speaking, the people ran away.
With gentle persuasion and considerable effort, he explained to them that he needed help.
After some time, several of them accompanied him back to the horse.
After a great deal of struggle, the animal was freed, although the horse was exhausted.
The sun had by then almost disappeared below the horizon, and the shadows of the trees had grown dark.
Louis then began walking back to the encampment and arrived there at approximately 9:00 p.m.
He indicated to the people who had accompanied him that they should go to his workers, and gave them a sheep to slaughter.
The people who had accompanied him naturally spent the night at the encampment.
(I will stop here for now, otherwise the day's entry will become too long.
Is it not remarkable how the “old people” — the Voortrekkers — such as Louis and the others were able to navigate and maintain their sense of direction in unfamiliar territory? And all of this while walking back alone to their encampment and their people with nothing more than a panga gun.)

1837
There are no entries for this day in the diary of Reverend Erasmus Smit.

Thursday, 27 September 1838
From the diary of Reverend Erasmus Smit.
Reverend Smit writes that he and his wife were short of meat that day.
Some of the other Voortrekkers noticed this and came to their assistance.
Several people in the laager also worked on the sod wall surrounding the camp.
(Maritz's laager, which stood directly opposite the reverend's laager on the opposite bank, had already been enclosed by a sod wall some time earlier.
It was this very sod wall around Maritz's laager that gave the camp its name, Sooilaer.
Later, with the addition of “Smit's laager,” both laagers were sometimes known collectively as Dubbele-Laer — “Double Laager.”)
The diary also mentions that the commandos returned that day, but without any confirmation of Zulus being in the area.
The Voortrekkers in the laagers had also seen three fires burning in the distance along the Tugela the previous day.
These fires gave rise to considerable speculation.

1862
General Louis Botha
General Louis Botha was born on this day at Greytown, Natal.
He is remembered as a general during the Anglo-Boer War, the first Prime Minister of the Union of South Africa, and founder of the Het Volk Party.

1886
Johannesburg / Marshalltown
Henry Brown Marshall submitted a request to the surveyor Kidgar Tucker.
Tucker was asked to survey and lay out Marshalltown, the oldest residential suburb of Johannesburg.
Johannesburg itself was at that stage little more than a mining camp and was still in the process of developing.

1893
Johannes Scheepers
Johannes Scheepers was born.
He is remembered as a founding member of the FAK (Federasie van Afrikaanse Kultuurvereniginge) and organising secretary of the Symbolic Ox-Wagon Trek of 1938.

Thursday, 27 September 1900
Anglo-Boer War
Day 352 of the war
Lord Roberts sent an official communication to Generals A. Hunter, L. Rundle and Bruce Hamilton:
“Clear the whole Free State of supplies and inform the burghers that if they choose to listen to De Wet and carry on a guerrilla warfare against us, they and their families will be starved.”
Lord Roberts wrote an official letter, for the second time, to General L. Botha.Lord Roberts stated that he had approximately 2,800 women and children at Pilgrim's Rest.He said that, because the Boers were continuing the struggle, he intended to send the women and children to General Botha and his commandos for their care.
General Beyers and Colonel L.J.A. Chapman became involved in a battle at Pienaars River Station.Colonel Chapman's artillery saved him from defeat.General Beyers's horse was shot and killed beneath him that day.
Commandant L.E. Keause sentenced 27 Boers for looting at Nylstroom and forced them back to the commandos.
At Elandskop near Heilbron, a member of the so-called Klaas Gang, a person of colour, was executed.This gang had made it their practice to terrorise women and children in the veld and on farms.Earlier that month the gang had been involved in a battle in which 12 of its members were killed and a further 18 summarily executed.
General Buller occupied Pilgrim's Rest.

Friday, 27 September 1901
Anglo-Boer War
Day 717 of the war
General Bruce Hamilton arrived at Fort Itala with 1,600 cavalrymen.He was under the impression that Chapman and the fort were in danger, and had covered 80 kilometres in 24 hours on a forced march.
Graaff-Reinet: The trials of Commandant J.C. Lotter, Lieutenant P.J. Wolfaardt, Field-Cornet W.S. Kruger, as well as J.C. Shoeman and D.C. Breedt, came to an end.All were sentenced to death on charges including high treason.
Commandant J.F.J. Dreyer became involved in a battle with Brigadier-General Bruce Hamilton at Mokari, near Vanstadensrus.
General J.C. Smuts crossed the railway line at Sheldon, near Port Elizabeth.

1970
South African Air Force — No. 2 Squadron
No. 2 Squadron of the South African Air Force, “The Flying Cheetahs,” departed Pretoria for Durban to take part in the Korean War.
No. 2 Squadron served as a wing of the United States Air Force during the war.
Of the 94 Mustangs, 74 were shot down, while of the 22 Sabres, four were shot down.
Thirty-four South African pilots were killed in the war.

1973
Johannes Frederikus van Wyk
Johannes Frederikus van Wyk died.
He is remembered as an outstanding teacher who often provided education to children free of charge.

text:
Mark his gamble of rejecting Iran's proposal to open the Strait of Hormuz in 7 days relying upon the potential of the MOU. Here is what this rejection reveals:

1- Proof that, after knowingly ripping off the MOU, the administration is killing its potential as well, potential that could have provided an off-ramp to end its war of aggression, turn the Strait of Hormuz back to normal, set the region, global economy, and energy free, and relieve American consumers at the pump.

2- Washington faces an undeniable strategic defeat, highly consequential for the world, yet its mindset remains entirely dogmatic: clinging to the illusions that max. pressure guarantees capitulation and that leverage is an exclusive U.S. privilege. By falling for its own lies, claiming that Iran is "losing so badly" and that the U.S. "controls" the Strait, the administration has become the primary obstacle to ending its own erratic war.

3- The administration’s narrative collapses under technical and military scrutiny: a) Moving 40 million barrels of crude through the Strait in 48 hours, amounting to pre-war baselines, is physically and technically a complete fabrication; b) As Iranian commanders have pointed out, if Washington truly "controls" the waterway, why is its navy absent? Independent maritime assessments confirm the U.S. blockade has withdrawn further out to sea to stay out of range of Iranian anti-ship missile systems; c) There is zero empirical evidence that Iran is buckling under pressure or relinquishing its strategic leverage.

4- The administration is paralyzed by an acute contradiction. The President desperately wants out before the midterm elections, but his ego demands he look like a winner, senselessly expecting Iran to simply absorb the costs and concede merely to save face.

5- Bitterly, a significant share of the current mess lies with U.S. allies who continue to accommodate Washington's "fly-by-wire" policies. The planned diplomatic track in Oman between Iran and neighboring countries, which could have offered Washington a face-saving bridge back to talks, was rendered moot. Interestingly, the same allies who blindly accommodate this administration recurrently end up burned by it.

Clinging to a coercive status quo is strategically bankrupt; leverage is never a one-way street. The only realistic exit is to abandon maximalist fantasies and pursue a soft landing. As FM Araghchi emphasized: "Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock." Iran remains steadfast.

text:
🏚️ 🎬 The Haunting in Connecticut (2009) • Movie Review 🎧🧧👁️
📽️ https://t.co/Fy25vUjjmX 

"A Dying Boy, a Borrowed House, and the Dead Who Never Left" 🕯️⚰️

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🗝️ ❝ We take a much more roundabout path, we spend more time in the borderland. ❞
     — Reverend Nicholas Popescu
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🌟 Hello again, dear listener!

Every haunted house story is really a story about a lease. Somebody signs something they shouldn't, in a hurry, for a price that's too good, and the rest is just the bill coming due.

What makes Peter Cornwell's 2009 debut worth your evening is that it knows exactly why this family signed. Sara Campbell is not renting a house. She is buying minutes — fewer hours in the car, more hours beside her son, in a year when hours are the only currency left. The house takes the deal. The house always takes the deal.

So the fear here arrives pre-loaded. Before a single door swings on its own, this family is already being haunted by something with a medical chart and a prognosis. The ghosts are late to their own picture. That's the trick, and it's a good one.

The chills land. But the ache is what stays. 💫

📍 Quick Movie Snapshot (specific, warm & honest)

🚗 1987. Sara Campbell (Virginia Madsen) drives her teenage son Matt (Kyle Gallner) home from an experimental cancer trial, and the long haul between hospital and kitchen table is quietly dismantling all of them.

🏠 She spots a man hammering a For Rent sign into the lawn of a big old Connecticut house. He is rattled. He wants it gone. He offers her the first month free if she signs today.

🪧 ❝ He said the place had a bit of a history. ❞
     — Sara Campbell, the understatement the whole film is built on

🛏️ The family moves in. Matt claims the basement, where a partition wall hides a locked door, while dad Peter (Martin Donovan), a recovering alcoholic, fights his own quiet war one floor up.

⚰️ The house was a funeral home. The room behind that locked door was the mortuary. Matt begins seeing an old bearded man, and corpses with symbols cut into their skin.

⛪ He confides in Reverend Nicholas Popescu (Elias Koteas), a fellow cancer patient from the hospital, who offers the only counsel that has ever worked in a ghost story: stop asking what it is. Ask what it wants.

📷 Cousin Wendy (Amanda Crew) turns up a box of séance photographs — a young medium named Jonah, ectoplasm streaming from his mouth — and a jar of dried human eyelids. Note the housekeeping of that detail. Somebody kept them. Somebody labeled the jar.

🔮 The trail leads to Ramsey Aickman, the mortician who ran the place and ran séances inside it, and to the night every soul in that room was found dead while Jonah simply stopped existing.

🔥 From there the house quits pretending. What Matt does to the walls in the final act is the image people still describe to each other seventeen years later, usually badly, usually with their hands.

🧭 Interesting Angles That Make This Movie Glow

💀 The premise is the kind of idea a writer waits a career for: a boy standing so near the exit that the dead recognize him as one of their own. It means the film's scariest idea and its saddest idea are the same idea, arriving in the same shot. The picture asks it out loud before a single ghost appears.

🙏 ❝ Why do bad things happen to good people? ❞
     — Sara Campbell, opening narration

👻 The séance photographs are not invented props. They come from the surviving archives of Thomas Glendenning Hamilton, a Canadian spiritualist who spent years photographing alleged ectoplasm in earnest. Those are real faces, really sitting in the dark in the 1920s, really believing. Nothing a production designer builds can match a genuine artifact of misplaced faith.

🎭 Virginia Madsen had read roughly twenty-five horror scripts and found nothing in them worth acting. She took this one for the family drama underneath the haunting, and it shows in the register she plays: not a screaming victim, but an exhausted woman doing math about her son's life expectancy in a hallway.

🤝 Madsen and Elias Koteas had shared a horror screen before, in The Prophecy (1995). That old familiarity is doing invisible work here. Two actors who already trust each other can make a conversation about death sound like a conversation between friends, which is the only way that scene survives.

⛓️ Consider what the film asks you to identify with. Not the mother, not the priest. A sick teenager who is being tortured by the dead and cannot tell anyone, because telling them would cost his family one more thing they can't afford. That silence is the real machinery of the picture.

🔗 Beautiful Ties Worth Celebrating

The alleged source case gives the fiction its spine: a family who moved into a former Southington, Connecticut funeral home in 1986 to be near their son's cancer treatment. Carmen Snedeker worked with the screenwriters across roughly two years of drafts, and whatever you conclude about the haunting, the circumstance was real and it was unbearable.

John Carpenter was attached to direct early on. The deal collapsed over creative differences, but the concept stayed with him — its tone and themes later drew him to The Ward. There is a version of this film in another universe with a Carpenter synth score, and horror fans will be arguing about it forever.

The picture is a Manitoba production wearing Connecticut clothes. It was shot in Teulon and Winnipeg, with most of the film staged inside a genuine 101-year-old house — real wood, real cold, real rooms that were tired long before the camera arrived.

And the architecture is the argument. Matt's bedroom and the mortuary are the same basement, divided by one thin partition and one locked door. The thing you are sleeping on top of was always there, a few feet away, behind a wall somebody built specifically so you wouldn't have to look at it. That is not a haunted house. That is a family.

🎥 What the Critics Say (All Positive, All Verifiable)

✍️ Tim Robey, The Telegraph — gave the film a favorable review, pointing to a strong emotional core and a solid script, and rating it the best haunted house film in some time.

✍️ Jim Vejvoda, IGN — reviewing out of SXSW, called the film effective despite its formula, crediting characters who are relatable and already in real peril from Matt's illness, which keeps viewers engaged as events turn fantastical.

✍️ Time Out — three out of five stars, calling it a dour, self-serious but surprisingly effective little haunted house shocker, and crediting Cornwell with holding it together and landing a decent scare every five to ten minutes.

💛 Why This Movie Feels So Special (Truth & Heart)

Audiences found this one and would not let go. It opened at number two in North America with roughly $23 million, finished at $55.4 million domestic and $78.8 million worldwide, then went straight to number one on the DVD and Blu-ray charts with about 1.5 million units sold in its first week. Home Media Magazine's 2009 Reaper Awards named it Best Ghost Story of the year. Ty Wood took a Young Artist Award for his turn as little brother Billy, and Virginia Madsen drew a Fangoria Chainsaw Awards nomination for Best Actress.

Critics split, and honestly so. The Tomatometer sits at 17 percent, and that number belongs in any truthful account of this film. But CinemaScore audiences graded it B−, and the gap between those two numbers is the most interesting thing about the picture.

Here is what the audience heard that the tally missed. Strip out the slammed doors and the grabbing hands and you still have a complete film underneath: a father white-knuckling his sobriety, a mother who would burn a house to the studs to keep her child, and a boy carrying a secret because he has calculated that his family cannot survive being told. The supernatural is the loud part. The grief is the load-bearing part.

The best ghost stories have always understood that a haunting is just grief with a floor plan. This one understands it too, even when it reaches for the cheap jolt — and it does reach, and you will jump, and that is a fair trade at nine o'clock on a dark night.

Watch for the séance photographs, and let yourself wonder about the people in them. Watch the quiet scenes between Matt and the reverend, two sick men talking plainly about what comes next, with none of the false comfort the genre usually hands out. And watch the small night scene where Matt sits out under the sky with his father.

⭐ ❝ Most of the stars we're seeing are already dead. ❞
     — Matt Campbell, and he knows exactly what he is looking at

That is the whole film in eleven words, spoken by a boy describing light that outlived its source. Then keep watching, because what Matt finds inside the walls turns an ordinary haunted rental into something closer to a mass grave with a mortgage — and turns a modest March horror release into the one your friends still bring up unprompted, all these years later.

🎧 Ready to dive in? Tap the link and let the Campbell house pull you under:
▶️ Watch Here — The Haunting in Connecticut (2009)

🚪 Next Door — The Haunting in Connecticut 2: Ghosts of Georgia (2013)

Before you go: there is a second door on this hallway, and almost nobody opens it.

Gold Circle announced a whole trilogy in June 2009 while the first film was still printing money. A Haunting in New York was planned and never made. What did arrive, in February 2013, was The Haunting in Connecticut 2: Ghosts of Georgia — and calling it a sequel is a small lie of marketing. New family. New state. New century of sorrow. The only thing it inherits is a title and a promise.

What it also inherits is Tom Elkins, who edited the first film and stepped up to direct this one — a man who already knew exactly where every scare in the original was buried, because he was the one who buried them. Ti West was attached before him, which is another haunted what-if for the pile.

This time the house sits in Ellerslie, Georgia, drawn from the alleged experiences of young Heidi Wyrick as recounted in The Veil: Heidi Wyrick's Story. The cast is a genuine surprise: Abigail Spencer, Chad Michael Murray, Katee Sackhoff, Emily Alyn Lind, and the great Cicely Tyson. And the history underneath the floorboards is not invented mortuary business but something far heavier and entirely American — the house was a stop on the Underground Railroad.

Sit with that for a second. The first film asked what a mortician did to the dead in his basement. The second asks what a country did to the living, and whether a house can hold that much.

It went out small — an $8 million picture, a limited theatrical run and video on demand, barely $5.1 million back. It never got the audience the first one found. Some of you have never heard of it until right now.

We're going through that door next. 🕯️

You're experiencing haunted-house craft done right — one locked door at a time.
See you on the other side for more love & discussion!

text:
There is a distinction between the Government and the State. When that distinction collapses, when the party in power begins to treat the permanent institutions of the State as extensions of its own political apparatus, democracy does not die in a single dramatic moment. It dies slowly, institution by institution, appointment by appointment, until citizens wake up one morning and discover that the State no longer belongs to them. It belongs to the party. We are approaching that morning.

The Government is temporary. It is the political leadership elected by the people for a defined term: the President, the Cabinet, and the members of Parliament. The Government sets policy. It proposes legislation. It makes political decisions. It answers to the electorate. And when the electorate decides it has had enough, the Government changes. This is the heartbeat of democracy: the peaceful transfer of power from one set of political leaders to another, with the understanding that the incoming government inherits not a blank slate, but a functioning State apparatus that serves the nation regardless of who holds office.

The State is permanent. It is the institutional infrastructure that exists before, during, and after any government: the judiciary, the military, the police, the civil service, the central bank, the electoral commission, the public prosecution service, the diplomatic corps, the anti-corruption agencies, the intelligence services, and the universities. These institutions do not belong to any political party. They belong to the people of Sri Lanka. Their officers swear oaths not to a party leader, but to the Constitution. Their function is to serve the republic, not the government of the day, but the republic as an enduring entity that transcends any election cycle.

The danger arises when a government, particularly one with an overwhelming parliamentary majority and a populist mandate, begins to erase the line between itself and the State; when the ruling party starts treating state institutions not as independent bodies to be respected, but as instruments to be captured, staffed with loyalists, directed toward partisan objectives, and weaponised against opponents; when "the government's anti-corruption commission" becomes "our commission"; when "the state broadcaster" becomes "our channel"; when "the judiciary" becomes "our courts"; and when "the military" becomes "our security apparatus." This is not governance. This is colonisation: the colonisation of the State by the party.

In Sri Lanka today, President Anura Kumara Dissanayake and several NPP ministers are systematically blurring the line between Government and State in ways that should alarm every citizen, regardless of political affiliation. The signs are everywhere. The Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption (CIABOC), a state institution that should operate with absolute independence, has been accused by its own targets of being staffed by individuals with JVP affiliations. The late Nandana Gunathilaka publicly identified the CIABOC Director General as a former member of the JVP's legal division. Whether that specific allegation is true or not, the perception that the state's anti-corruption body is an extension of the ruling party is itself a catastrophic failure of institutional independence. When citizens believe that CIABOC investigates enemies of the JVP and ignores allies of the JVP, when cases against the Leader of the Opposition are quietly dropped while cases against Rajapaksa-aligned figures are pursued with maximum force, the institution ceases to function as a state body and becomes a partisan weapon.

The judiciary, the most critical of all state institutions, is now under direct threat. The 22nd Amendment, passed with the government's two-thirds majority, extends the tenure of sitting judges, including the Chief Justice who presided over the very determination that cleared its passage. Four Supreme Court vacancies have been left unfilled for over a year while the government selectively extends the careers of judges already on the bench. The Bar Association has been sidelined. The Commonwealth Lawyers Association has raised alarms. The UN Special Rapporteur's questions went unanswered. The message to every judge in the country is unmistakable: your career depends on the government's willingness to legislate it. That is not an independent judiciary. That is a judiciary on a government leash.

The police and intelligence services, which should serve the State, not the party, continue to engage in surveillance, intimidation, and reprisals against civil society actors, journalists, and human rights defenders, as documented by the UN Human Rights Council in its September 2026 report. The CID questions people about their travel to Geneva. Intelligence officers threaten individuals who participate in UN reviews. A journalist was questioned by the CID, which then contacted Twitter to demand the deletion of her tweets. This is not the State protecting national security. This is the party using the state security apparatus to monitor, intimidate, and silence those who challenge the Government.

This is not without precedent. History offers devastating examples of what happens when the line between Government and State is erased.

In Venezuela, Hugo Chávez came to power in 1999 with a genuine popular mandate and a promise to transform a corrupt political system. He then systematically captured every state institution: packing the Supreme Tribunal with loyalists, politicising the military by promoting ideologically aligned officers, turning the state oil company PDVSA into a party funding mechanism, replacing independent civil servants with political appointees, and using state media as a propaganda arm. By the time Nicolás Maduro inherited the system, there was no State left, only the party. When the economy collapsed, when inflation reached millions of percent, and when millions of Venezuelans fled the country, there were no independent institutions left to check the government, hold it accountable, or facilitate a peaceful transfer of power. The State had been consumed by the party, and the people had nothing left to turn to. Venezuela is not a failed state because of sanctions or imperialism. It is a failed state because a popular government erased the distinction between Government and State, and by the time the people realised what had happened, there was no institution left that answered to them rather than to the party.

In Hungary, Viktor Orbán's Fidesz party won a two-thirds parliamentary majority in 2010, the same supermajority the NPP holds in Sri Lanka today. Orbán did not abolish democracy. He hollowed it out from within. He packed the Constitutional Court with loyalists, changed the rules for judicial appointments to ensure ideologically aligned judges, placed allies at the head of the prosecution service so that corruption investigations targeted opponents and ignored allies, took control of state media and allowed allied oligarchs to purchase private media outlets, rewrote electoral laws to favour his party, and staffed the civil service with political appointees who owed their careers to Fidesz rather than to the State. Elections still happen in Hungary. The opposition can still campaign. But the State, the institutional infrastructure that should be neutral, serves the party. The European Union has formally classified Hungary as a "hybrid regime" and an "electoral autocracy." Orbán achieved this not through a military coup, but through the patient, methodical capture of state institutions by a party with a parliamentary supermajority and a populist mandate. The parallels with Sri Lanka are not subtle.

In Turkey, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's AKP came to power in 2002 promising democratic reform, economic modernisation, and an end to the old establishment's corruption. For the first decade, the AKP delivered genuine economic growth and institutional reform. But gradually, Erdoğan began treating the State as an extension of his party. After the 2016 coup attempt, he purged over 150,000 civil servants, judges, military officers, academics, and teachers, not because all of them were coup plotters, but because the crisis provided the pretext to replace independent state officials with loyal party members. The judiciary was packed. The central bank lost its independence. The intelligence services became instruments of presidential power. Universities were brought under political control. Today, Turkey holds elections, has opposition parties, and maintains the formal architecture of democracy, but the State serves the President, not the people. The independent institutions that should check executive power have been captured so thoroughly that they function as departments of the ruling party.

In Poland, the Law and Justice Party (PiS) used its parliamentary majority between 2015 and 2023 to systematically capture the judiciary by changing the composition of the Constitutional Tribunal, creating a new disciplinary chamber to punish independent judges, and politicising judicial appointments. The European Court of Justice ruled that Poland's judicial reforms violated EU law. When a new government was elected in 2023, it discovered that reversing institutional capture was extraordinarily difficult: PiS-appointed judges remained on the bench, PiS-aligned prosecutors remained in office, and the State institutions that had been captured continued to resist the new government's authority. This is the most important lesson Poland offers Sri Lanka: institutional capture is easy to execute but nearly impossible to reverse. Once a party's loyalists are embedded in the judiciary, the prosecution service, the anti-corruption agencies, and the civil service, they remain there long after the party loses power. The damage is structural and generational.

In Zimbabwe, the example about which Commonwealth Lawyers Association President Steven Thiru specifically warned Sri Lanka, the government fast-tracked a constitutional amendment to raise the Chief Justice's retirement age from 70 to 75 precisely when the sitting Chief Justice was about to reach the mandatory retirement age. The amendment was presented as a general reform. It was, in reality, a tailor-made extension for a specific judge who had demonstrated loyalty to the ruling ZANU-PF party. Thiru warned that this "fundamentally undermined institutional credibility." Sri Lanka's 22nd Amendment follows the same pattern: a retirement age extension, rushed through Parliament, that directly benefits the sitting Chief Justice who was appointed by the current President and who presided over the determination that cleared the amendment's passage.

What connects Venezuela, Hungary, Turkey, Poland, and Zimbabwe is not ideology. Chávez was a socialist. Orbán is a right-wing nationalist. Erdoğan is an Islamist conservative. PiS was Catholic-nationalist. Mugabe was a liberation-era autocrat. They have nothing in common politically except one thing: each of them used a popular mandate and a parliamentary majority to systematically erase the distinction between Government and State. Each of them captured the judiciary, politicised the prosecution service, weaponised anti-corruption agencies against opponents, brought the security services under partisan control, and staffed state institutions with loyalists. And in each case, by the time the public understood what was happening, the institutions that could have stopped it had already been captured.

Sri Lanka is not yet Hungary, Turkey, or Venezuela. But the trajectory is visible: a government with 159 seats and no effective parliamentary opposition; a judiciary whose tenure has just been legislated by the government and whose vacancies are being strategically left unfilled; an anti-corruption commission whose independence is questioned; intelligence services that surveil civil society on behalf of the party; a government that conflates criticism of the party with treason against the State; ministers who speak of state institutions as though they are party departments; and a President who tells rally crowds that he is "blindfolded," while his government's blindfold is carefully adjusted to see some targets and not others.

text:
Healing Through Water, Strength Through Solidarity 🌊

Today at Nehru Stadium, Chennai, a free hydrotherapy session transformed a swimming pool into a powerful space of healing, dignity, and hope for individuals living with muscular dystrophy. 

In this unique therapeutic environment, water is not used for recreation; it serves as a vital clinical tool to reduce the harsh load of gravity, ease chronic pain, relax tight muscles, and protect remaining physical strength.

Muscular dystrophy is a group of genetic conditions causing progressive muscle wasting, with Duchenne (DMD) being the most severe childhood form.

Because India lacks a comprehensive public registry, under-diagnosis is common, and families spend years searching for answers. 

The burden is immense, stairs become mountains, schools become inaccessible, and mothers often leave employment to provide round-the-clock care. 

This is a critical public health and social justice issue, not a private misfortune.
While Tamil Nadu provides a ₹2,000 monthly allowance and central policies offer rare-disease funds, lifelong care demands far more. 

We urgently need a state-wide registry, early genetic screening, decentralized district-level therapy centers, and inclusive education that never abandons a child.

Highest praise to the exceptional organizing body, partners, and tireless volunteers who built this circle of solidarity today. 

They refused to let these families suffer in isolation, setting a golden standard for community-driven healthcare. 

To the brave children: your body may have physical limits, but your dreams have none. To the parents: you are not carrying this load alone. Awareness without action is merely noise, a state’s conscience must be filled with compassion every single day. 💙

Poland could pay up to 17 billion zloty ($4.4 billion) for a permanent base on its territory, the presidential National Security Bureau (BBN) has said. The project, which is currently being discussed with Washington, involves a facility that could house 5,000 troops, the agency told the newspaper Rzeczpospolita this week.
Warsaw offered to host a permanent US base during President Donald Trump’s first term in 2018, proposing to name the facility ‘Fort Trump.’ Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski confirmed this week that a deal on the base was nearing completion.
Deputy Defense Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who traveled to the US this week for the talks on the base among other things, stated that the final decision rests with Trump and that she did not expect it to be made before the review of the posture of US forces, which is expected to be finalized in November or December. According to the BBN, the base could be completed in 2029 under “optimal conditions.”
Under Trump, Washington has pressed European NATO members to boost defense spending and take on more responsibility for arming Ukraine while the US concentrates resources on competing with China. The US is also widely expected to scale back its military presence in Europe as part of this strategy shift.
America still considers Poland a “model ally,” according to US Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby, the man behind the US policy shift that has since become known as ‘NATO 3.0.’ Sobkowiak-Czarnecka also told journalists this week she had heard “many warm words from the American side acknowledging our preparedness and motivation.”
The US already has a permanent Army garrison and command headquarters in the city of Poznan, although most of the 10,000 US troops stationed in the country serve on a rotational basis. According to Deputy Defense Minister Stanislaw Wziatek, this number could grow to 15,000, with 5,000 stationed permanently at the new base.
Warsaw has been one of Kiev’s most ardent supporters in its ongoing conflict with Moscow. It also serves as a key logistics hub for delivering Western military aid to Ukraine while also bordering the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad to the northeast.
Tensions between Moscow and Warsaw recently flared as Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski vowed to inflict a swift defeat upon Russia in case of a direct clash with NATO. “If Russia attacked us and we took our gloves off, I think we would defeat Russia quite quickly,” he stated in mid-September, prompting Nikolay Patrushev, an aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin, to warn that Poland could “cease to exist” within days if it undertakes military action against Russia and forces Moscow to use its full arsenal.
