text:
The Crown Arrived Before the Consent
The young king died, and a kingdom began to mourn. He had made the throne feel close to its people: youthful, gentle, a symbol of peace and belonging. While they were still speaking his name through tears, others were already measuring the seat he had left behind.
For years, some of the loudest voices in the succession had been remarkably quiet about the kingdom’s needs. They had offered little support to the young king, little gratitude for what he and his mother had carried. Now, suddenly, they spoke as guardians of its future. Their first tribute to the dead was to compare him with a proposed successor and announce how much better things would be. Insults aimed at the late king and the queen mother passed as honest debate. A mild question about the new candidate, however, was treated as an offense against culture.
There was an indicated heir, but those entrusted with the succession looked elsewhere. He was young, they said, as though royalty had ever required a child to govern alone, or a regent had never held a kingdom steady until an heir came of age. To those watching, it seemed less an objection to his age than a convenient way to close the door on his line. The elder with authority over the process had neither the resources for a prolonged contest nor much affection for the late king’s mother. Old resentment from the years she had held influence found a useful disguise: custom. Revenge put on ceremonial robes and demanded respect.
Then the state arrived with support for the mourning, a substantial contribution to the coronation, and a car and cash offered to the elder as “appreciation.” Perhaps each gift could be explained on its own. Together, amid a contested succession and a kingdom short of funds, they raised an uglier question: had the custodians of the crown sold the independence that made their voices worth hearing? In trying to display their power, they exposed how cheaply it might be courted.
The ruling clan pressed ahead while others were pushed aside. Every objection received a lecture on tradition; every exception received a convenient explanation. The young king’s Christianity had once been held against him as insufficiently traditional. His proposed successor was also Christian—and a preacher at that—but suddenly faith posed no difficulty at all. Custom appeared less like a principle than a gate opened for friends and bolted against opponents.
The questions multiplied. Why disregard the indicated heir? Why demand such haste that the throne could scarcely be allowed an empty hour? Why was the army so visible in a matter said to belong to the palace? Why discourage the heir’s side from seeking a court’s judgment? Around the proposed king stood connections to powerful soldiers and the president’s family. Supporters campaigned for acceptance as though legitimacy were a vote to be whipped. Even the would-be king sought attendance at his own coronation. The crown was being advertised with the urgency of a rally.
Meanwhile, the queen mother became a target. She had lived through more of the palace’s history than many of its newest lecturers on custom, and perhaps that made her inconvenient. They tried to tarnish her name, though many people continued to stand by her. Those who defended the late king or questioned the succession were mocked, shunned or pressed to be silent. It was a peculiar court where disrespect towards the dead was freedom of speech, but scrutiny of the living was sacrilege.
The spectacle revealed more than a disputed succession. It showed elders willing to trade credibility for influence, factions mistaking access to government for the people’s consent, and too many hands reaching into the same royal pot. Some who claimed to defend the kingdom seemed chiefly determined to settle scores or secure a place near power. Their pride could not conceal their lack of preparation.

Seven years of bombardment failed to destroy the Houthi forces. Neither did the 2022 ceasefire. Instead, the ceasefire served as a window of opportunity for the Houthis to regroup, expand their ranks, and upgrade their arsenal. By 2026, this force—once derisively nicknamed the "slipper army"—had emerged as the most powerful non-state armed group in the Middle East; it possessed missiles with ranges exceeding 1,600 kilometers, drones capable of threatening Red Sea shipping, and effective control over strategic locations surrounding the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The ceasefire was not the end, but a turning point.
The UN-brokered ceasefire of April 2022 marked the first nationwide truce in six years. In a briefing to the Security Council, the UN Special Envoy acknowledged that the ceasefire was "broadly holding" and that civilian casualties had dropped significantly. However, the agreement did not disarm the Houthis of their missiles and drones, nor did it require them to cede territory. It merely "paused" the most intense fighting.

What did the Houthis do during this period? Peter Salisbury, an associate professor at Columbia University, offered a crucial assessment: "After the 2022 Yemen ceasefire agreement took effect, the volume of weapon-manufacturing materials entering Yemen surged, and the number of transport routes multiplied."

text:
Trump rejected Iran's conditional offer to restore normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz within seven days. The clock starts only if the U.S. accepts the plan; no ceasefire or reopening has been agreed.

The September 26 rejection follows mediated U.S.–Iran discussions earlier in the week that Trump called productive. Iran sent its proposal to Washington through Qatar. Trump said he rejected the deal but gave no detailed public account of which terms he opposed. He described Iran as wanting to open the strait immediately, a different account from Iran's conditional timetable.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said normal maritime passage could resume within seven days if Washington accepted the plan and its necessary conditions were met. The reported package included ending the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, relief from sanctions on Iranian oil sales and a ceasefire covering Lebanon. It also contemplated renewed nuclear negotiations.

The proposed sequence remains unsettled. Accounts place reopening on day six or seven; another describes seven days as a window for U.S. acceptance before talks. No definitive day-by-day proposal has been authenticated. The seven-day period is not a deadline already running.

Araghchi said Tehran would wait for an official U.S. position through mediators before deciding its next move. For now, some vessels and oil are getting through Hormuz, but normal commercial passage has not returned. Roughly one-fifth of the world's oil and gas normally passes through the strait. Whether diplomacy produces an agreed ceasefire and reliable passage remains unresolved.

text:
Iran Is Losing Latin America: Colombia Signals a Strategic Shift in the Western Hemisphere

Colombia may be the clearest example of the dramatic geopolitical shift now taking place across Latin America, and of the increasingly difficult environment Iran faces in the Western Hemisphere.

Only a few years ago, under Gustavo Petro, Bogotá maintained diplomatic relations and political engagement with Tehran. Today, the picture could hardly be more different. Colombia has formally severed diplomatic relations with the Islamic Republic and separately designated Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organization. The Colombian government explicitly framed these decisions in terms of national and hemispheric security, transnational crime, and alleged Iranian links to terrorist and narcoterrorist organizations.

Colombia is therefore important not simply because of the bilateral relationship. It illustrates a broader political realignment taking place across parts of Latin America. As governments on the right have gained influence, several countries have sought closer strategic relations with Washington. In this environment, their approach toward Iran is increasingly becoming part of a wider debate about security, organized crime, terrorism, and the future of U.S. influence in the Western Hemisphere.

From Tehran’s perspective, this represents another significant setback for an Iranian foreign policy that has invested heavily in expanding relationships across the Global South. Latin America offered Iran diplomatic partners, economic opportunities, and political space far beyond the Middle East. That space is now becoming more constrained.

But severing diplomatic relations or designating the IRGC is only part of the challenge. Governments concerned about Iranian activities will also have to decide how they approach the broader infrastructure through which Tehran has historically sought influence: religious and cultural institutions, Iranian-linked educational networks,  including Al-Mustafa International University, financial channels, relationships with local actors, and the activities of Iranian diplomatic missions.

The financial dimension deserves particular attention. Authorities should examine potential channels for moving funds connected to Iran or Hezbollah, including cryptocurrency, alongside conventional financial networks and possible connections to transnational criminal organizations. These issues require evidence-based investigation rather than treating every Iranian-linked religious, cultural, or commercial institution as inherently illicit.

The same applies to Iranian embassies. Diplomatic missions are legitimate institutions, but where governments have specific security concerns, counterintelligence and law-enforcement agencies should scrutinize activities that may extend beyond conventional diplomacy while distinguishing documented conduct from allegation.

The larger strategic picture is becoming increasingly difficult for Tehran. Iran still retains important relationships in Latin America, particularly with governments such as Cuba and Nicaragua, while Brazil remains a major regional power that maintains diplomatic relations and significant channels of engagement with Tehran. But Iran's political room for maneuver across much of the hemisphere is narrower than it was only a few years ago.

For the administration, this development also has broader significance. The emerging alignment is not simply about Iran. It reflects a renewed emphasis on hemispheric security and on the strategic competition over influence in Latin America. Whether this becomes something resembling a modern version of the Monroe Doctrine will depend on how U.S. policy develops, but Iran increasingly finds itself caught in that broader realignment.

For years, Tehran believed that its relationships across the Global South could offset Western diplomatic and economic pressure. Latin America was an important part of that strategy. Colombia's dramatic reversal demonstrates how quickly that assumption can change, and how much more contested Iran's position in the Western Hemisphere has become.

There are no unconditional grants — there never been.

But there are conditions, and there are traps — and there are conditions that are traps.

If someone offered you $10M grant, but told you that:

1. You must leave your front and back doors open permanently.

2. You must remove protein from your meals.

3. You must marry your daughter to the village's never-do-well.

4. Most importantly, you must use the $10M to buy goods at 20-40% higher than market price at the stores of the donor's choosing.

...amongst other egregious ''conditions'.

You might think, "ehn... Even after the wicked conditions, I'll live like a king from the $10M"

WRONG!❌

The $10 million never actually enters your bank account. It never becomes liquidity.

The benefactor announces the grant, everybody hails him, you fulfill the debilitating conditions, he releases the money...

More claps and photoshoots...

...and then immediately routes that same money through the open back door straight back into his own pocket to pay for the overpriced goods you were forced to buy.

So more than what you the money bought, you'll find that your doors are open, your children are malnourished, your precious daughter is married off to the abusive villain...

And your pocket is empty.

This is exactly how Oyinbo plays the game with Africa.

They announce a "$100 Million Development Grant" in the news. The Western public claps. The African politicians smile and take their cut. 

But under the table, the conditions of that grant dictate that an African nation must slash its health budget, sell its electricity dams to foreign companies for pennies, and hire only Western contractors who charge triple the price.

The money basically takes a flight from Washington, touches down in an African central bank for five minutes, and flies right back to Europe.

The West gets the praise, the corporations get the cash, the corrupt politicians get their kickbacks, and the ordinary African is left with a massive debt, a broken economy, no sovereignty — and a silver bullet that kills his arguments in a debate about Western villainy.

I've not told you how bad it is. I just used easy words to explain what I said before because I want you to understand it.

text:
Ted Weschler was born in 1962 in Buffalo and grew up moving around the industrial Midwest, especially Erie, Pennsylvania. 

He was the youngest of five. In middle school he wrote that he wanted to be a millionaire.

He graduated from Wharton in 1983. A classmate had already told him to read everything Buffett wrote. Buffett became a hero.

His first job was junior financial analyst at W.R. Grace. Pay: $22,000. The moment he could join the company retirement plan, he put in the maximum and took every dollar of the company match. 

When he left in 1989, the account was worth about $70,000. He moved it into a self directed IRA so he could pick the stocks himself. In 1990 it fell 52%. He treated that as a lesson, not a reason to stop.

In 2000 he launched his own hedge fund, Peninsula Capital, from a two room office above a bookstore. Short sleeves and shorts. No Wall Street costume. He owned a handful of stocks and held them for years. DaVita, the dialysis company he had studied since his Grace days, was a signature bet.

From early 2000 until he closed the fund in 2011, early investors made about 1,236%, or about 22% a year after fees, while the broader market barely moved. Peninsula grew to about $2 billion.

His personal IRA kept compounding. By 2012 it was about $131 million. He converted it to a Roth and paid about $28 million in taxes so future growth would be tax free. By the end of 2018 it was about $264 million. 

Every holding, he said, was a public stock anyone could have bought. The same $70,000 in an S&P 500 fund would have been about $2 million by 2021. The rest came from picking a few stocks with care and giving them time.

Every year a San Francisco charity auctions a meal with Buffett. In 2010 an anonymous bidder paid about $2.5 million. In 2011 the same bidder paid about $2.5million again. Both bidders were Weschler. Total: about $5 million, all for charity.

Weschler got a long office visit and a three hour dinner with Buffett. At the second meal, while Weschler looked at his notes, Buffett said he would be a good fit at Berkshire.

Weschler panicked. The offer was not on his script. He did not say no. Within weeks he said yes, closed the fund, kept his home in Charlottesville, and started flying to Omaha at his own expense. 

Buffett later said money was not the reason Weschler came. He was already making plenty. Admiration was.

He joined Berkshire in 2012 to run a slice of the stock portfolio. Deep research. A few big bets. Long holds. He still reads odd trade magazines looking for what the crowd misses.

8 Things You Need to Know about Surveillance
8 important truths about surveillance
ai-in-society
Author
Rachel Thomas

Published
August 7, 2019

Over 225 police departments have partnered with Amazon to have access to Amazon’s video footage obtained as part of the “smart” doorbell product Ring, and in many cases these partnerships are heavily subsidized with taxpayer money. Police departments are allowing Amazon to stream 911 call information directly in real-time, and Amazon requires police departments to read pre-approved scripts when talking about the program. If a homeowner doesn’t want to share data from their video camera doorbell with police, an officer for the Fresno County Sheriff’s Office said they can just go directly to Amazon to obtain it. This creation of an extensive surveillance network, the murky private-public partnership surrounding it, and a lack of any sort of regulations or oversight is frightening. And this is just one of many examples related to surveillance technology that have recently come to light.

I frequently talk with people who are not that concerned about surveillance, or who feel that the positives outweigh the risks. Here, I want to share some important truths about surveillance:

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
Data often contains errors
Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
Surveillance changes our behavior
Surveillance disproportionately impacts the marginalized
Data privacy is a public good
We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
While I was writing this post, a number of investigative articles came out with disturbing new developments related to surveillance. I decided that rather than attempt to include everything in one post (which would make it too long and too dense), I would go ahead and share the above facts about surveillance, as they are just a relevant as ever.

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
There is a long history of data about sensitive attributes being misused, including the use of the 1940 USA Census to intern Japanese Americans, a system of identity cards introduced by the Belgian colonial government that were later used during the 1994 Rwandan genocide (in which nearly a million people were murdered), and the role of IBM in helping Nazi Germany use punchcard computers to identify and track the mass killing of millions of Jewish people. More recently, the mass internment of over one million people who are part of an ethnic minority in Western China was facilitated through the use of a surveillance network of cameras, biometric data (including images of people’s faces, audio of their voices, and blood samples), and phone monitoring.

Adolf Hitler meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. in 1937. Source: Computer History
Pictured above is Adolf Hitler (far left) meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. (2nd from left), shortly before Hitler awarded Watson a special “Service to the Reich” medal in 1937 (for a timeline of the Holocaust, see here). Watson returned the medal in 1940, although IBM continued to do business with the Nazis. IBM technology helped the Nazis conduct detailed censuses in countries they occupied, to thoroughly identify anyone of Jewish descent. Nazi concentration camps used IBM’s punchcard machines to tabulate prisoners, recording whether they were Jewish, gay, or Gypsies, and whether they died of “natural causes,” execution, suicide, or via “special treatment” in gas chambers. It is not the case that IBM sold the machines and then was done with it. Rather, IBM and its subsidiaries provided regular training and maintenance on-site at the concentration camps: printing off cards, configuring machines, and repairing them as they broke frequently.

Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
In the above examples, the data collection began before genocide was committed. IBM began selling to Nazi Germany well before the Holocaust (although continued for far too long), including helping with Germany’s 1933 census conducted by Adolf Hitler, which was effective at identifying far more Jewish people than had previously been recognized in Germany.

It is important to recognize how data and images gathered through surveillance can be weaponized later. Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote that “One [hard truth] is that data and surveillance networks created for one purpose can and will be used for others. You must assume that any personal data that Facebook or Android keeps are data that governments around the world will try to get or that thieves will try to steal.”

Plenty of data collection is not involved with such extreme abuse as genocide; however, in a time of global resurgence of white supremacist, ethno-nationalist, and authoritarian movements, it would be deeply irresponsible to not consider how data & surveillance can and will be weaponized against already vulnerable groups.

Data often has errors (and no mechanism for correcting them)
A database of suspected gang members maintained by California law enforcement officials was found to be full of errors, including 42 babies who had been added to the database when they were less than 1 year old (28 of whom were marked as “admitting to being gang members”). Even worse, there was no process in place for correcting mistakes or removing people once they’ve been added.

An NPR reporter recounts his experience of trying to rent an apartment and discovering that TransUnion, one of the 3 major credit bureaus, incorrectly reported him as having two felony firearms convictions. TransUnion only removed the mistakes after a dozen phone calls and notification that the story would be reported on. This is not an unusual story: the FTC’s large-scale study of credit reports in 2012 found 26% of consumers had at least one mistake in their files and 5% had errors that could be devastating. An even more opaque, unregulated “4th bureau” exists: a collection of companies buying and selling personal information about people on the margins of the banking system (such as immigrants, students, and people with low incomes), with no standards on what types of data are included, no way to opt out, and no system for identifying or correcting mistakes.

Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
What makes the examples in the previous section disturbing is not just that errors occurred, but that there was no way to identify or correct them, and no accountability for those profiting off the error-laden data. Often, even the existence of the systems being used is not publicly known (much less details of how these systems work), unless discovered by journalists or revealed by whistleblowers. The Detroit Police Dept used facial recognition technology for nearly two years without public input and in violation of a requirement that a policy be approved by the city’s Board of Police Commissioners, until a study from Georgetown Law’s Center for Privacy & Technology drew attention to the issue. Palantir, the defense startup founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, ran a program with New Orleans Police Department for 6 years which city council members did not even know about, much less have any oversight.

After two studies found that Amazon’s facial recognition software produced inaccurate and racially biased results, Amazon countered that the researchers should have changed the default parameters. However, it turned out that Amazon was not instructing police departments that use its software to do this either. Surveillance programs are operating with few regulations, no oversight, no accountability around accuracy or mistakes, and in many cases, no public knowledge of what is going on.

8 Things You Need to Know about Surveillance
8 important truths about surveillance
ai-in-society
Author
Rachel Thomas

Published
August 7, 2019

Over 225 police departments have partnered with Amazon to have access to Amazon’s video footage obtained as part of the “smart” doorbell product Ring, and in many cases these partnerships are heavily subsidized with taxpayer money. Police departments are allowing Amazon to stream 911 call information directly in real-time, and Amazon requires police departments to read pre-approved scripts when talking about the program. If a homeowner doesn’t want to share data from their video camera doorbell with police, an officer for the Fresno County Sheriff’s Office said they can just go directly to Amazon to obtain it. This creation of an extensive surveillance network, the murky private-public partnership surrounding it, and a lack of any sort of regulations or oversight is frightening. And this is just one of many examples related to surveillance technology that have recently come to light.

I frequently talk with people who are not that concerned about surveillance, or who feel that the positives outweigh the risks. Here, I want to share some important truths about surveillance:

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
Data often contains errors
Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
Surveillance changes our behavior
Surveillance disproportionately impacts the marginalized
Data privacy is a public good
We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
While I was writing this post, a number of investigative articles came out with disturbing new developments related to surveillance. I decided that rather than attempt to include everything in one post (which would make it too long and too dense), I would go ahead and share the above facts about surveillance, as they are just a relevant as ever.

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
There is a long history of data about sensitive attributes being misused, including the use of the 1940 USA Census to intern Japanese Americans, a system of identity cards introduced by the Belgian colonial government that were later used during the 1994 Rwandan genocide (in which nearly a million people were murdered), and the role of IBM in helping Nazi Germany use punchcard computers to identify and track the mass killing of millions of Jewish people. More recently, the mass internment of over one million people who are part of an ethnic minority in Western China was facilitated through the use of a surveillance network of cameras, biometric data (including images of people’s faces, audio of their voices, and blood samples), and phone monitoring.

Adolf Hitler meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. in 1937. Source: Computer History
Pictured above is Adolf Hitler (far left) meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. (2nd from left), shortly before Hitler awarded Watson a special “Service to the Reich” medal in 1937 (for a timeline of the Holocaust, see here). Watson returned the medal in 1940, although IBM continued to do business with the Nazis. IBM technology helped the Nazis conduct detailed censuses in countries they occupied, to thoroughly identify anyone of Jewish descent. Nazi concentration camps used IBM’s punchcard machines to tabulate prisoners, recording whether they were Jewish, gay, or Gypsies, and whether they died of “natural causes,” execution, suicide, or via “special treatment” in gas chambers. It is not the case that IBM sold the machines and then was done with it. Rather, IBM and its subsidiaries provided regular training and maintenance on-site at the concentration camps: printing off cards, configuring machines, and repairing them as they broke frequently.

Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
In the above examples, the data collection began before genocide was committed. IBM began selling to Nazi Germany well before the Holocaust (although continued for far too long), including helping with Germany’s 1933 census conducted by Adolf Hitler, which was effective at identifying far more Jewish people than had previously been recognized in Germany.

It is important to recognize how data and images gathered through surveillance can be weaponized later. Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote that “One [hard truth] is that data and surveillance networks created for one purpose can and will be used for others. You must assume that any personal data that Facebook or Android keeps are data that governments around the world will try to get or that thieves will try to steal.”

Plenty of data collection is not involved with such extreme abuse as genocide; however, in a time of global resurgence of white supremacist, ethno-nationalist, and authoritarian movements, it would be deeply irresponsible to not consider how data & surveillance can and will be weaponized against already vulnerable groups.

Data often has errors (and no mechanism for correcting them)
A database of suspected gang members maintained by California law enforcement officials was found to be full of errors, including 42 babies who had been added to the database when they were less than 1 year old (28 of whom were marked as “admitting to being gang members”). Even worse, there was no process in place for correcting mistakes or removing people once they’ve been added.

An NPR reporter recounts his experience of trying to rent an apartment and discovering that TransUnion, one of the 3 major credit bureaus, incorrectly reported him as having two felony firearms convictions. TransUnion only removed the mistakes after a dozen phone calls and notification that the story would be reported on. This is not an unusual story: the FTC’s large-scale study of credit reports in 2012 found 26% of consumers had at least one mistake in their files and 5% had errors that could be devastating. An even more opaque, unregulated “4th bureau” exists: a collection of companies buying and selling personal information about people on the margins of the banking system (such as immigrants, students, and people with low incomes), with no standards on what types of data are included, no way to opt out, and no system for identifying or correcting mistakes.

Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
What makes the examples in the previous section disturbing is not just that errors occurred, but that there was no way to identify or correct them, and no accountability for those profiting off the error-laden data. Often, even the existence of the systems being used is not publicly known (much less details of how these systems work), unless discovered by journalists or revealed by whistleblowers. The Detroit Police Dept used facial recognition technology for nearly two years without public input and in violation of a requirement that a policy be approved by the city’s Board of Police Commissioners, until a study from Georgetown Law’s Center for Privacy & Technology drew attention to the issue. Palantir, the defense startup founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, ran a program with New Orleans Police Department for 6 years which city council members did not even know about, much less have any oversight.

After two studies found that Amazon’s facial recognition software produced inaccurate and racially biased results, Amazon countered that the researchers should have changed the default parameters. However, it turned out that Amazon was not instructing police departments that use its software to do this either. Surveillance programs are operating with few regulations, no oversight, no accountability around accuracy or mistakes, and in many cases, no public knowledge of what is going on.

A Heartfelt Tribute to Dr. Manmohan Singh

Today, as I stand and reflect on my life journey, I cannot separate my story from the story of India's economic transformation.

I was born in 1986 into a remote tribal family living in extreme poverty. My parents struggled to raise nine children. We lived in a small hut, often uncertain about our next meal. Food was scarce, and rice was a luxury for us. Many nights, I cried for rice. Our family survived mainly on ragi, wheat, millets, roots, and forest produce. I still remember how my younger uncle would save a plate of rice for me every night and morning because he knew how much I longed for it.

Those were difficult days. Poverty was not a statistic for us. It was a daily reality.

Yet, through government schools, tribal welfare hostels, educational opportunities, and the expanding aspirations of a changing India, my life slowly transformed. My brother and I joined a tribal Ashram school. Education opened a door that poverty could not close. Step by step, that journey eventually led me to the Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati.

When I look back, I see more than my personal struggle. I see the impact of policies that empowered millions of ordinary Indians. I see the vision of leaders who believed that even the poorest child in the remotest village deserved an opportunity.

Among those leaders, Dr. Manmohan Singh occupies a special place.

At a critical moment in India's history, when the nation faced a grave economic crisis, Dr. Manmohan Singh helped lay the foundation for a stronger, more resilient, and self-confident India. Through wisdom, integrity, and economic foresight, he contributed to opening new opportunities for generations of Indians. His work helped create an environment where talent, regardless of birthplace or background, could aspire to something greater.

For people like me, his contributions are not merely economic reforms. They are stories of hope. They are stories of children who moved from huts to universities, from poverty to possibility, from survival to dignity.

I remain deeply grateful to the vision and contributions of leaders such as Jawaharlal Nehru, Indira Gandhi, Rajiv Gandhi, P. V. Narasimha Rao, and especially Dr. Manmohan Singh, whose leadership helped shape modern India's economic architecture.

The statue of Dr. Manmohan Singh in Hyderabad is not just a monument of stone and metal. It is a symbol of gratitude. It represents the dreams of millions of Indians whose lives were transformed by opportunity. It honors a statesman of remarkable humility, a distinguished scholar, an economist of global stature, and a leader who believed in the power of knowledge, hard work, and inclusive progress.

For millions of families who rose from poverty, Dr. Manmohan Singh's legacy lives not only in economic data or policy documents, but in our homes, our education, our aspirations, and our achievements.

As someone who once cried for a plate of rice and later walked the halls of IIT Guwahati, I offer my deepest respect and gratitude.

Thank you, Dr. Manmohan Singh. Your legacy is written not merely in history books, but in the lives of millions of Indians who dared to dream and were given a chance to succeed.

Kind regards 

Ravi Gedela, Ph.D.
Ph.D in Biosciences and Bioengineering, @IITGuwahati
M. Tech in Biotechnology @IITGuwahati

text:
🪷 Agastya Rishi, Devi Lopamudra Tarpanam 🪷

Agastya Rishi Tarpanam (and Arghya Danam) is a sacred Hindu ritual performed on Bhadrapada Purnima (the full moon day just preceding Pitru Paksha). Historically, the tradition commemorates the annihilation of the demons Atapi and Vatapi by Sage Agastya, making this offering a necessary prelude to ancestral worship. Performing this ritual ensures that the ancestors remain satisfied and do not wander in search of water throughout the year.

Phase 1: Agastya Rishi Arghya & Tarpanam Ritual
According to traditional scriptural injunctions, the libation to Sage Agastya is offered while facing the South (the direction of the star Agastya/Canopus rising in the southern sky). The ritual is performed with both feet touching the ground or immersed in water.

First Arghya
Original Script: 
ॐ कुम्भयोनिर्महातेजास्तपसा पुष्करेक्षणः । 
उद्यन्ते लङ्काद्वारेऽर्घ्यं प्रतिगृह्यताम् ॥

Phonetic Transliteration: 
Om Kumbhayonir-Mahātejās-Tapasā Puṣkarekṣaṇaḥ |
Udyante Laṅkā-Dvāre-'Arghyaṁ Pratigrṛhyatām ||

Translation: Oh Sage born from the pitcher, possessor of great divine effulgence, whose eyes resemble lotuses bloomed through intense penance; as you rise at the gates of Lanka, please accept this sacred water offering (Arghya).

Second Arghya
Original Script: 
ॐ शङ्खपुष्पफलोतोयँ रत्नानि विविधानि च ।
उद्यन्ते लङ्काद्वारेऽर्घ्यं प्रतिगृह्यताम् ॥

Phonetic Transliteration: 
Om Śaṅkha-Puṣpa-Phalo-Toyaṁ Ratnāni Vividhāni Ca |
Udyante Laṅkā-Dvāre-'Arghyaṁ Pratigrṛhyatām ||

Translation: I offer this water contained in the conch shell, mixed with flowers, fruits, and symbolic diverse gems. As you rise at the gates of Lanka, please accept this offering.

Third Arghya
Original Script: 
ॐ कासपुष्पप्रतीकाश वह्निमारुतसम्भव ।
उद्यन्ते लङ्काद्वारेऽर्घ्यं प्रतिगृह्यताम् ॥

Phonetic Transliteration: 
Om Kāsa-Puṣpa-Pratīkāśa Vahni-Māruta-Sambhava |
Udyante Laṅkā-Dvāre-'Arghyaṁ Pratigrṛhyatām ||

Translation: Oh Sage who gleams brightly like the white Kaas flower, born through the divine combination of Fire (Agni) and Wind (Marut); as you rise at the gates of Lanka, please accept this offering.

Prayer to Sage Agastya
Original Script: 
ॐ आतापिभक्षितो येन वातापिश्च महाबलः ।
समुद्रः शोषितो येन स मेऽगस्त्यः प्रसीदतु ॥

Phonetic Transliteration: 
Om Ātāpi-Bhakṣito Yena Vātāpiś-Ca Mahābalaḥ |
Samudraḥ Śoṣito Yena Sa Me-'Agastyaḥ Prasīdatu ||

Translation: May that great Sage Agastya be pleased with me—he who consumed the demon Atapi and digested the highly powerful demon Vatapi, and who completely drank and dried up the mighty ocean.

Phase 2: Lopamudra Tarpanam (Offering to his Consort)
Immediately following the offerings to Sage Agastya, a libation is traditionally offered to his wife, Devi Lopamudra, to honor the sacred feminine principle of their lineage.

Original Script: 
ॐ लोपामुद्रे महाभागे राजपुत्रि पतिव्रते ।
मया दत्तमिदमर्घ्यं प्रतिगृह्यताम् ॥

Phonetic Transliteration: 
Om Lopāmudre Mahābhāge Rājaputri Pativrate |
Mayā Dattam-Idam-Arghyaṁ Pratigrṛhyatām ||

Translation: Oh highly auspicious Devi Lopamudra, the virtuous princess and devoted wife; please accept this sacred water offering presented by me.

Traditional Guidelines & Prerequisites
Materials Required: A clean copper vessel or conch shell filled with water, white flowers, unbroken rice grains (Akshata), seasonal fruits (such as cucumber), Kaas flowers, and Kusha grass.
Posture and Orientation: Face the South direction. Unlike the standard Pitru Tarpan where the sacred thread (Janeu) is worn over the right shoulder (Apasavya), for the Agastya Arghya, one stays Savya (normal placement over the left shoulder) or assumes Malakar (hanging like a necklace) depending on the regional manual being followed. Keep both feet touching the ground or in the water.
Timing: Performed on the noon/afternoon of Bhadrapada Purnima, right at the seasonal cusp of Pitru Paksha.

🪷🙏 Hari 🕉 🙏🪷

text:
Early last year I drove my 2017 Pajero through the same University of Ibadan gates I once walked through with nothing but dreams and my parents’ blessings.

I entered UI with nothing but dreams. I left UI with a First Class Honours in Law and the same dreams, only heavier.  
I returned bearing gifts.

The Faculty of Law had become family. First stop was the Dean. He was glad to see me. He prayed. I told him what God had placed in my heart for the Faculty — a foundation. He agreed to serve as a trustee, blessed me as a father would, and sent me on.

The second stop mattered more. I had lost contact. She had not seen me in nearly fifteen years. I did not call. I simply appeared at her flat on campus.

She asked who it was. 
I gave my name. The door opened. Then she saw me. We caught up quickly. She was preparing for her inaugural lecture and time was short. Still, I took her to the Pajero. Rice, Indomie, spaghetti. A small thank-you for a large debt.

She is Prof. Bukola Ruth Akinbola. My mother in the academia. My mentor. The one who secured my full tuition scholarship from Faith Foundation in Jericho from Year 2 to Year 5. The one who prevailed on Hon. Justice Prof. Alero Akeredolu PhD 
to reach the former Attorney-General, Chief Akinlolu Olujinmi, SAN, CON, who then gave me a full Nigerian Law School scholarship. The same Prof. who told me, after Year 3, to stay away from politics because my CGPA was crying. That advice saved the First Class. I later taught her son in her own home.

She blessed me that afternoon. Then she looked at the Pajero 
and expressed concern about driving it back to Ikire, Irewole Local Government, Osun State. Not so much the town. The village people who, she believed, had tracked my movements since childhood. She has spiritual oversight. She knows me. I left UI that day with a lighter vehicle and a fuller heart. Double blessing. I would remember her words sooner than I expected.

After UI, I lodged in Ibadan, then drove with a friend to my mother’s project site in her hometown. As firstborn, I had taken the lead: 
two plots, fencing, foundation, skeletal work up to roofing. All seemed well until that afternoon.

On the road, trying to connect to the express, 
I met an angry mob. 
My first instinct was to reverse. I had not seen the bus behind me. 
A slight dent, barely visible. I came down, pleaded, offered ₦50,000, then ₦100,000 to settle and leave before the crowd reached us.

The driver refused. 
He began to shout.

I went back to the Pajero, changed sneakers for slippers, asked my guest to step out, and locked the SUV. By then some of the men — masked, some not — were closer. One of the leaders asked why we were standing there.

I answered in Yoruba:  
“Ke pe o baba mi. Omo yin la je. Accident kekere lo se le…” 

My father, I am your child. It was a minor accident. I was trying 
to avoid you.

Safety mattered 
more than pride.

That same day, I later read, a similar mob killed the local government chairman of the town. 
I was shaken. 
How close I had come, 
in my mother’s own hometown.

There was also an accountability problem with the person acting as project manager — funds that could not be explained, a few million still claimed for work 
I had never agreed to take on credit. I made the uneasy call to pull back.

I forgot the site. Until a conversation with my siblings. My sister told me the rest of them had quietly come together and completed the house without telling me or troubling me. I was amazed. Grateful. In moments like that you see who family is.

That was one mercy. There were others.

A good friend, then a student at Bayero University Kano, whose father was an Admiral — some said the first four-star of that description — warned me not to drive from Kano to Katsina. 

Prof. Akinbola had already warned me about the Pajero and Ikire. Two different people. Two different roads. Same grace.

[Cont'd]

“Ke pe o baba mi. Omo yin la je. Accident kekere lo se le…” 

My father, I am your child. It was a minor accident. I was trying 
to avoid you.

Safety mattered 
more than pride.

That same day, I later read, a similar mob killed the local government chairman of the town. 
I was shaken. 
How close I had come, 
in my mother’s own hometown.

There was also an accountability problem with the person acting as project manager — funds that could not be explained, a few million still claimed for work 
I had never agreed to take on credit. I made the uneasy call to pull back.

I forgot the site. Until a conversation with my siblings. My sister told me the rest of them had quietly come together and completed the house without telling me or troubling me. I was amazed. Grateful. In moments like that you see who family is.

That was one mercy. There were others.

When I mentioned it to another member, she said I was being entitled and that serving the man of God shouldn't come with expectations of a meal

Now half the team thinks I'm disrespectful for even bringing it up

What’s Irritating About Luther

Our own flaws irritate us the most when we see them in someone else. Is that the case with Lutheranism?
Lutherans have undergone an evolution. They, too, once had confessionals and the Apocrypha in their Bibles. They were integrated into the state apparatus just like Catholics; without baptism in their church, one could not be a citizen, and without a wedding there, one’s children were bastards. I imagine a newcomer from across the eastern border cannot tell one church from the other. You have to calmly explain the differences between *trans*- and *con*-substantiation (good luck with that!) or give a discreet wink: "That lady over there is the pastor's wife." Why pay a premium if you can't see the difference? — one might be tempted to ask.

The world's first Lutheran state was established on Polish soil, by the grace of the Polish king reigning there at the time.

Did Lutherans not, in fact, do to Catholics the very same thing that Catholics did to the pagan religion of Rome? Of course they did!

The greatest, most glaring artifact of pagan times is the altar-priest-sacrifice triad. Nothing has changed there. From the perspective of an ordinary service attendee, the rest is merely rebranding. The Mother of God is now called Mary—fine. Is Dionysus now called Hubert? That doesn't matter; what counts is that the game remains the same.

Of course, I could cite theological arguments here—reminding everyone that the matter of altar sacrifices and priests was settled once and for all by the single sacrifice offered in the heavenly temple; and, to top it off, the prophesied and executed judgment that "not one stone would be left upon another" effectively meant a bloodbath for the priests and faithful Jews defending the temple and the altar.

The power of the old religion was—and is—so potent that it compelled even(!) the Apostle Paul, its zealous opponent, to appear in the Jewish temple to offer a sacrifice. Fortunately, God did not allow this to happen, and Paul subsequently had plenty of time to reflect on it—in prison. You are, of course, familiar with the texts I am referring to.

In closing—Luther, much like Paul before him, ultimately yielded to the pressures of his time. To me, they are heroes of the faith. And the mills of history keep on grinding.

Marek

Luke 11:1-54

1 And it came to pass, that, as he was praying in a certain place, when he ceased, one of his disciples said unto him, Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples.
2 And he said unto them, When ye pray, say, Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, as in heaven, so in earth.
3 Give us day by day our daily bread.
4 And forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation; but deliver us from evil.
5 And he said unto them, Which of you shall have a friend, and shall go unto him at midnight, and say unto him, Friend, lend me three loaves;
6 For a friend of mine in his journey is come to me, and I have nothing to set before him?
7 And he from within shall answer and say, Trouble me not: the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give thee.
8 I say unto you, Though he will not rise and give him, because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth.
9 And I say unto you, Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.
10 For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened.
11 If a son shall ask bread of any of you that is a father, will he give him a stone? or if he ask a fish, will he for a fish give him a serpent?
12 Or if he shall ask an egg, will he offer him a scorpion?
13 If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children: how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?
14 And he was casting out a devil, and it was dumb. And it came to pass, when the devil was gone out, the dumb spake; and the people wondered.
15 But some of them said, He casteth out devils through Beelzebub the chief of the devils.
16 And others, tempting him, sought of him a sign from heaven.
17 But he, knowing their thoughts, said unto them, Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation; and a house divided against a house falleth.
18 If Satan also be divided against himself, how shall his kingdom stand? because ye say that I cast out devils through Beelzebub.
19 And if I by Beelzebub cast out devils, by whom do your sons cast them out? therefore shall they be your judges.
20 But if I with the finger of God cast out devils, no doubt the kingdom of God is come upon you.
21 When a strong man armed keepeth his palace, his goods are in peace:
22 But when a stronger than he shall come upon him, and overcome him, he taketh from him all his armour wherein he trusted, and divideth his spoils.
23 He that is not with me is against me: and he that gathereth not with me scattereth.
24 When the unclean spirit is gone out of a man, he walketh through dry places, seeking rest; and finding none, he saith, I will return unto my house whence I came out.
25 And when he cometh, he findeth it swept and garnished.
26 Then goeth he, and taketh to him seven other spirits more wicked than himself; and they enter in, and dwell there: and the last state of that man is worse than the first.
27 And it came to pass, as he spake these things, a certain woman of the company lifted up her voice, and said unto him, Blessed is the womb that bare thee, and the paps which thou hast sucked.
28 But he said, Yea rather, blessed are they that hear the word of God, and keep it.
29 And when the people were gathered thick together, he began to say, This is an evil generation: they seek a sign; and there shall no sign be given it, but the sign of Jonas the prophet.
30 For as Jonas was a sign unto the Ninevites, so shall also the Son of man be to this generation.
31 The queen of the south shall rise up in the judgment with the men of this generation, and condemn them: for she came from the utmost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and, behold, a greater than Solomon is here.
32 The men of Nineve shall rise up in the judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it: for they repented at the preaching of Jonas; and, behold, a greater than Jonas is here.
33 No man, when he hath lighted a candle, putteth it in a secret place, neither under a bushel, but on a candlestick, that they which come in may see the light.
34 The light of the body is the eye: therefore when thine eye is single, thy whole body also is full of light; but when thine eye is evil, thy body also is full of darkness.
35 Take heed therefore that the light which is in thee be not darkness.
36 If thy whole body therefore be full of light, having no part dark, the whole shall be full of light, as when the bright shining of a candle doth give thee light.
37 And as he spake, a certain Pharisee besought him to dine with him: and he went in, and sat down to meat.
38 And when the Pharisee saw it, he marvelled that he had not first washed before dinner.
39 And the Lord said unto him, Now do ye Pharisees make clean the outside of the cup and the platter; but your inward part is full of ravening and wickedness.
40 Ye fools, did not he that made that which is without make that which is within also?
41 But rather give alms of such things as ye have; and, behold, all things are clean unto you.
42 But woe unto you, Pharisees! for ye tithe mint and rue and all manner of herbs, and pass over judgment and the love of God: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.
43 Woe unto you, Pharisees! for ye love the uppermost seats in the synagogues, and greetings in the markets.
44 Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are as graves which appear not, and the men that walk over them are not aware of them.
45 Then answered one of the lawyers, and said unto him, Master, thus saying thou reproachest us also.
46 And he said, Woe unto you also, ye lawyers! for ye lade men with burdens grievous to be borne, and ye yourselves touch not the burdens with one of your fingers.
47 Woe unto you! for ye build the sepulchres of the prophets, and your fathers killed them.
48 Truly ye bear witness that ye allow the deeds of your fathers: for they indeed killed them, and ye build their sepulchres.
49 Therefore also said the wisdom of God, I will send them prophets and apostles, and some of them they shall slay and persecute:
50 That the blood of all the prophets, which was shed from the foundation of the world, may be required of this generation;
51 From the blood of Abel unto the blood of Zacharias which perished between the altar and the temple: verily I say unto you, It shall be required of this generation.
52 Woe unto you, lawyers! for ye have taken away the key of knowledge: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered.
53 And as he said these things unto them, the scribes and the Pharisees began to urge him vehemently, and to provoke him to speak of many things:
54 Laying wait for him, and seeking to catch something out of his mouth, that they might accuse him.

ELON Treasury Co.

A company built for the moment business leaves Earth’s edge.

Space is no longer a trailer. It is infrastructure.

Satellites are already a multi-hundred-billion-dollar industry. Starlink, national constellations, and Earth-observation networks are turning orbit into the new utility layer. The Moon is shifting from a flag-planting destination to a staging ground: power, mining, logistics, and return tickets. Mars is policy, engineering, and capital allocation — not a bedroom poster.

Every new economy needs three things: energy, transport, and a way to settle value.
The first two are being built now. The third is still unclaimed.

Our thesis is simple.

Dogelon Mars ($ELON) is not only a meme. It is one of crypto’s most consistent stories about money for the next planet. For more than five years the project has held the same line: Mars, interplanetary trade, a community that calls itself Martians. Behind the lore there is more than copy: an L2, a Mars metaverse, and an early chapter in which the community helped fund space-adjacent research.

We do not claim a token automatically becomes legal tender on Mars.
We claim that the most recognizable “currency of Mars” carries extreme optionality on the day a space economy needs a digital unit of account, a brand, and a ready-made nation of believers.

What the company does

•  Accumulates $ELON as its core thesis asset

•  Holds ETH as the counterweight: liquidity, borrowable collateral, and a bridge into the established crypto economy

•  Does not sell the thesis for short-term cash flow

•  Offers a clean corporate wrapper so others can own the exposure without managing keys themselves

Why this, why now
 Space companies are already priced as if the future is arriving. Satellite cash flows, lunar contracts, and orbital logistics are being underwritten years before a permanent base exists. Capital has started moving from “someday” to “what is already positioned?”
Most people chase rockets and land.
We chase the thing rockets and land will eventually be priced in.

The upside

If the space economy is only a larger satellite and defense market, the ETH reserve and the discipline keep the company alive.
If the story hits — if the next commercial zone is called Luna, Gateway, or Mars — then an early, concentrated position in the most recognized interplanetary token is not a joke. It is a call option on an entirely new market.
We are not buying a dream because it is charming.
We are buying it because the stage is already under construction.
*To Mars. With a balance sheet.*

text:
[Scene]

A highly realistic candid photograph outside a small traditional Japanese neighborhood restaurant on a bright late-September afternoon.

The restaurant has a warm wooden storefront, white noren curtains, potted green plants, a handwritten menu board, and a vertical wooden “営業中” sign beside the entrance.

The pavement directly outside has just been washed and is still wet, with shallow patches of water and soft reflections catching the sunlight.

Warm afternoon sunlight enters from the side, creating gentle highlights on the women, the wet pavement, and the wooden storefront.

The atmosphere feels ordinary, warm, slightly playful, and spontaneous, like a friend happened to photograph a tiny inconvenience on the way home.

[Subjects]

Two Japanese young adult women, age 18–20.

Both have clear, natural youthful adult female faces, dark hair, minimal makeup, realistic skin texture, and understated everyday appearances.

Their bodies have healthy, balanced, realistic proportions with natural leg thickness, ordinary shoulder and hip proportions, and believable muscle and body-fat distribution.

No fashion-model proportions, extremely thin legs, exaggerated waists, elongated limbs, or oversized heads.

Hands, fingers, arms, legs, ankles, feet, toes, and all joints are anatomically correct and naturally positioned.

[Clothing]

Both women wear modest Japanese summer school uniforms: white short-sleeved cotton blouses with navy ribbon bows, knee-length navy pleated skirts, plain white crew socks, and simple black leather penny loafers.

The uniforms have realistic cotton texture, natural wrinkles, and ordinary signs of wear.

Both carry simple dark school backpacks.

[Woman A]

Woman A stands on the left.

After stepping across the freshly washed pavement, she notices that moisture and dye from inside her loafer have left a small dark gray mark around the underside and heel area of her white sock.

She balances naturally on her left leg while bending forward at the waist.

Her right knee is raised in front of her, bringing her socked right foot upward where she can inspect it closely.

Her left foot remains firmly planted on the wet pavement in its black loafer.

She holds the removed right loafer loosely in her left hand beside her raised leg.

With her right hand, she gently pinches the edge of her white sock near the stained heel, turning it slightly to inspect the mark.

Her expression is mildly puzzled and amused rather than distressed.

[Woman B]

Woman B crouches naturally on the right side, close to her friend.

Both of her feet remain fully inside her black loafers and rest naturally on the pavement.

She holds several slightly crumpled wet tissues in both hands and offers them upward toward Woman A.

She tilts her head slightly upward and looks at her friend with a small amused smile, clearly reacting to the unexpected stain.

Her posture is relaxed and practical, as though she has just offered to help clean the sock.

[Interaction]

The relationship between the two women should be immediately readable.

Woman A is inspecting the stained sock while balancing above her friend.

Woman B stays close beside her, looking upward and offering tissues.

Their eye lines, hand positions, and physical distance clearly connect the two actions into one spontaneous shared moment.

[Composition and Camera]

Vertical 4:5 composition.

A moderately low three-quarter side view, photographed from several steps away at approximately knee-to-waist camera height.

Both women are the clear main subjects and large enough in the frame to show expressions and small details.

Show both women completely from the tops of their heads to the bottoms of their feet.

Woman A’s standing foot, raised socked foot, removed loafer, both legs, both hands, and entire body must be visible.

Woman B’s complete crouching body, both legs, both shoes, both hands, and entire body must also be visible.

Do not crop or substantially obscure any feet, shoes, socks, legs, hands, or heads.

Keep every visible foot anatomically connected to the correct woman.

[Photography Style]

Authentic Japanese everyday youth photography, natural friend snapshot, photorealistic.

Realistic skin pores and subtle imperfections, natural dark hair, detailed cotton fabric, realistic white sock fibers, slightly worn black leather loafers, wet pavement texture, and believable reflections.

Warm natural afternoon sunlight with soft highlights and realistic shadows.

Moderate natural depth of field: subjects clearly detailed while the restaurant background remains recognizable rather than heavily blurred.

Restrained warm colors, subtle film grain, gentle old-photo feeling, and realistic dynamic range.

The image should feel like an ordinary memory captured accidentally rather than a planned fashion photograph.

No commercial advertising aesthetic, glamour posing, plastic skin, HDR, CGI, anime appearance, exaggerated bokeh, teal-and-orange grading, excessive sharpening, or artificial studio lighting.

Outsourcing companies made an estimated £6bn in profit from public services last year, with close to 11% of all public expenditure going to these private firms.

A new report by the think tank Common Wealth found that the public sector spent £129bn on services provided by outsourcing firms, despite the Labour government pledging to bring more public services in-house.

Since the 1980s, private companies have increasingly been brought in to run services once offered by the state. It was hoped that these supposedly efficient firms could break up cumbersome state-owned monopolies. 

But the influx of private companies has just created new monopolies. Serco – which has a £2bn contract with the Royal Navy and also manages public bicycle hire schemes – gets 90% of its global revenue from public sector contracts, according to Common Wealth’s research. 

Meanwhile, outsourcing giants have faced numerous scandals over the years. Back in 2020 G4S was fined £44m by the Serious Fraud Office after overcharging the Ministry of Justice for tagging offenders, some of whom had died. 

Common Wealth found that around 1.3 million people are employed by these firms in the UK, which is over seven times the number of police officers in the country. Many of these workers are in low-paid jobs, as the pressure to win public contracts forces wages down, even as their bosses get huge salaries. Former Serco CEO Mark Irwin, for example, reportedly earned £845,000 a year. 

Report author Sophie Flinders said: “For too long the government has allowed outsourcing giants Mitie, Serco and Sodexo to grow rich from worsening living standards. Public sector-wide insourcing would restore decent work for over a million people across the country. The government should work with the unions to make insourcing a reality.”

Donald Trump’s decision to reject Iran’s seven-day proposal and his  expectation of renewed US bombing after the November midterms raise the possibility that Washington is preparing to return to open-ended military escalation rather than pursue the diplomatic off-ramp now on the table. The timing matters because Iran has offered a defined sequence: US de-escalation and relief from the naval blockade and oil sanctions, reopening the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, followed by renewed nuclear negotiations. Trump rejected the proposal on 26 September.

That decision comes after a significant military development on 5 September. Iranian forces launched ballistic missiles towards two US warships near the Strait of Hormuz. US officials described subsequent attacks as close calls, while Iran claimed it had tested newer anti-ship capabilities. Iranian officials have associated the operation with the Qassem Basir, a missile unveiled in 2025 with a stated range of about 1,200 km and manoeuvrable re-entry capability. Independent assessments have not established that the Qassem Basir definitely struck or damaged a US warship.

The 5 September incident is being discussed again because the Pentagon has now added 37 wounded personnel, including 29 sailors and eight Marines, to its Iran-war casualty database, taking the recorded wounded total to 861. The Pentagon has not identified when or where those injuries occurred, so linking the 37 cases directly to the September 5 naval confrontation remains unsubstantiated.

The strategic significance is broader than one missile exchange. US naval forces enforcing pressure on Iran operate inside a contested missile environment, while Iran possesses geographic proximity, a large missile inventory and leverage over the world's most important energy chokepoints. The Strait normally carries roughly one-fifth to one-quarter of global oil flows, giving any prolonged confrontation consequences well beyond the Gulf.

This explains why the September 5 episode has acquired renewed significance. It demonstrated that military pressure on Iran does not remove Iran's capacity to impose costs on US forces and global energy markets. Tehran is now combining that military leverage with a diplomatic proposal that offers a concrete route towards reopening Hormuz and restarting nuclear negotiations.

The central strategic question is therefore whether Washington seeks an agreement that reduces the conflict or a renewed campaign designed to extract further concessions. If bombing resumes after the midterms, the September 5 confrontation will be remembered not as an isolated naval episode but as an early indication of the escalation risks surrounding any attempt to impose a settlement through sustained military coercion.

text:
Kaja Kallas says that Russia’s escalating attacks on Europe reflect Moscow’s weakness rather than its strength.

It is a convenient formula.

But history shows that weakness and danger can coexist perfectly well.

For decades, great powers have tried to avoid fighting one another directly. Instead, they fought through allies, proxies, weapons, money, intelligence services, and the territory of third countries.

Korea. Vietnam. Afghanistan. Later, Syria.

These were very different conflicts, and reducing them to a single formula would be misleading. But one pattern keeps returning: great-power rivalry is usually paid for most heavily by the people whose land becomes the battlefield.

The Soviet Union withdrew from Afghanistan in 1989 after almost a decade of war. The government Moscow had supported survived for several more years before collapsing in 1992.

The United States ended its direct military involvement in Vietnam after the Paris Peace Accords in 1973. Two years later, South Vietnam collapsed, and the world watched the helicopter evacuation from Saigon. More than 58,000 American servicemen had been killed.

In 2021, Afghanistan delivered another version of the same lesson.

Washington had spent years building and financing a state and its security forces. Yet in August, provincial capitals fell one after another. President Ghani fled. The government and security forces effectively collapsed. The Taliban entered Kabul.

Syria became an even more complicated version of the same game.

Russia, Iran, the United States, Turkey, and other outside powers spent years backing different forces while pursuing their own strategic interests. Bashar al-Assad’s government depended heavily on Russian and Iranian support. It eventually collapsed in December 2024 after a rapid rebel offensive — a strategic blow to the influence of its external backers.

Now the centre of confrontation is Ukraine.

Putin himself has gone as far as saying that, in his interpretation of history, “all of Ukraine is ours.”

The West describes its support for Ukraine in terms of sovereignty, European security, and the international order.

At the same time, the strategic interests of states have not disappeared: energy, logistics, defence industries, trade, and influence still matter.

And now something fundamental has changed.

Europe is no longer simply watching this kind of struggle unfold somewhere else.

Cyber operations.

Sabotage.

Attacks on critical infrastructure.

Information warfare.

Airspace violations.

These are no longer distant events. They are becoming part of Europe’s own security environment.

So perhaps the question — “Is this Russian strength or Russian weakness?” — is simply too narrow.

The more interesting question is this:

Are we watching a new game?

Or the same old game of great powers — only moving closer to home?

Vietnam, Afghanistan, and Syria all offer an uncomfortable lesson.

Great powers often enter conflicts with simple explanations: security, freedom, stability, historical justice.

They usually leave with consequences far more complicated than anything they promised at the beginning.

Kallas is right about one thing: the threat is real.

But perhaps the most important question is not how strong Moscow is today.

It is whether Europe truly understands what kind of historical game it has already entered — and what happens when the board is no longer somewhere far away, but increasingly on its own soil.

♦️ The October election could open the door to changes in Israel’s regional policies. Much will depend on the next government and US efforts to reduce conflicts around Israel. However, the post-October 7 security approach is likely to remain influential.

♦️ October 7 has fundamentally shaped Israel’s security worldview. The prevailing view is that threats should be addressed before reaching Israeli territory, based on adversaries’ capabilities and stated positions rather than assumptions about their intentions.

♦️ Israel’s military actions have come with diplomatic costs. Operations in Gaza, Lebanon, Syria and Iran have weakened diplomatic support, while relations with Türkiye and Saudi Arabia have deteriorated.

♦️ A new government could adopt more moderate policies after the election. But any government would still face pressure to maintain the post-October 7 security approach, making major policy shifts difficult.

♦️ Gaza and Lebanon remain complicated despite ceasefire agreements. Israel doubts Hamas will fully disarm in Gaza. In Lebanon, it questions whether the government and Lebanese Armed Forces can secure areas from which Israel withdraws while Hezbollah refuses to disarm.

♦️ Syria offers greater potential for de-escalation. A return to the 1974 Israel-Syria agreement and an Israeli withdrawal from areas seized after Assad’s fall could theoretically be possible, although Israel still has significant security concerns.

♦️ Iran and Türkiye present different challenges. Washington now leads efforts to contain Iran, and Israel recognises that it cannot easily confront Tehran without US support. Türkiye may be more difficult because of growing regional competition and tensions over Syria and Gaza.

Proposed Russian Role in the Gulf Settlement

Russia could help make the settlement harder to break by combining Security Council diplomacy, direct engagement with Iran, and a limited maritime presence. Its purpose would be to protect an agreed ceasefire and civilian navigation, while giving the United States a credible path to restrain any ally that threatens the agreement.

1. Negotiate the mandate. Russia should work with the United States, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Iran, and other Council members on a resolution requiring safe civilian passage through Hormuz, reciprocal nonaggression, and independent investigation of attacks. Russia’s recent diplomatic contact with Iran makes it a plausible participant in this effort, though it cannot guarantee Iranian compliance on its own. https://t.co/rVa3Zh0WKo

2. Offer a conditional naval contribution. If the coastal states agree and a clear mandate exists, Russia could offer vessels to a joint maritime monitoring mission. Their role would be observing shipping incidents, maintaining communication with other naval commands, and helping protect designated civilian passage under common rules. Russia should not deploy a unilateral fleet to confront Israel or the U.S.; that could turn a regional ceasefire into a great-power crisis.

3. Create a rule against sabotage. The mission should record and independently assess any attack that threatens shipping or the ceasefire, regardless of whether the alleged perpetrator is Israel, Iran, an aligned armed group, or another state. Consequences would follow an agreed review process, rather than a naval commander deciding which country to punish.

4. Give Washington room to act independently. In your proposal, the alleged coercion of Trump, military leaders, and politicians can be stated as an allegation warranting investigation. The immediate policy safeguard is a public U.S. commitment: American forces, intelligence, and offensive assistance will not support an operation that violates the settlement. Russia’s role would help verify events, while the U.S. makes its own decision about its support.

Suggested language for “Trust the Plan”:

Russia should be invited to support a negotiated Gulf settlement as a Security Council participant and maritime guarantor. Subject to the consent of the relevant coastal states and an agreed international mandate, Russia may contribute naval vessels to a jointly governed mission protecting civilian navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. Those vessels shall operate under common deconfliction rules, report incidents for independent review, and neither threaten Israel nor obstruct lawful shipping.The mission shall apply the same rules to every party. Its purpose is to preserve an open Strait and prevent any government or armed force from collapsing the agreement through unilateral attacks. The United States shall retain independent control over its military decisions and decline support for operations that breach the settlement.
The key choice is a Russian contribution to a joint mission, rather than Russia becoming the force that “contains Israel.” That gives Russia a meaningful role without making a naval confrontation the enforcement mechanism.

A stronger version of your plan would give Trump a public, defensible basis for restraint: a Gulf-led agreement, verified rules applying to Israel and Iran alike, and an explicit U.S. decision not to support operations that break it. Russia could back that agreement at the Security Council and participate in maritime monitoring under agreed rules.

That puts the decision where it belongs: Washington can support Israel’s civilian defense while declining to support a particular offensive operation. It does not need a Russian fleet to establish that choice.

text:
Surveillance changes our behavior
Hundreds of thousands of people in Hong Kong are protesting an unpopular new bill which would allow extradition to China. Typically, Hong Kong locals use their rechargeable smart cards to ride the subway. However, during the protests, long lines of people waited to use cash to buy paper tickets (usually something that only tourists do) concerned that they would be tracked for having attended the protests. Would fewer people protest if this was not an option?

In the United States, in 2015 the Baltimore Police Department used facial recognition technology to surveil people protesting the death of Freddie Grey, a young Black man who was killed in police custody, and arrested protesters with outstanding warrants. Mass surveillance could have a chilling impact on our rights to move about freely, to express ourselves, and to protest. “We act differently when we know we are ‘on the record.’ Mass privacy is the freedom to act without being watched and thus in a sense, to be who we really are,” Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote in the New York Times.

Flyer from the company Geofeedia Source
Surveillance disproportionately impacts those who are already marginalized
Surveillance is applied unevenly, causing the greatest harm to people who are already marginalized, including immigrants, people of color, and people living in poverty. These groups are more heavily policed and surveilled. The Perpetual Line-Up from the Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology studied the unregulated use of facial recognition by police, with half of all Americans appearing in law enforcement databases, and the risks of errors, racial bias, misuses, and threats to civil liberties. The researchers pointed out that African Americans are more likely to appear in these databases (many of which are drawn from mug shots) since they are disproportionately likely to be stopped, interrogated, or arrested. For another example, consider the contrast between how easily people over 65 can apply for Medicare benefits by filling out an online form, with the invasive personal questions asked of a low-income mother on Medicaid about her lovers, hygiene, parental shortcomings, and personal habits.

In an article titled Trading privacy for survival is another tax on the poor, Ciara Byrne wrote, “Current public benefits programs ask applicants extremely detailed and personal questions and sometimes mandate home visits, drug tests, fingerprinting, and collection of biometric information… Employers of low-income workers listen to phone calls, conduct drug tests, monitor closed-circuit television, and require psychometric tests as conditions of employment. Prisoners in some states have to consent to be voiceprinted in order to make phone calls.”

Data privacy is a public good, like air quality or safe drinking water
Data is more revealing in aggregate. It can be nearly impossible to know what your individual data could reveal when combined with the data of others or with data from other sources, or when machine learning inference is performed on it. For instance, as Zeynep Tufekci wrote in the New York Times, individual Strava users could not have predicted how in aggregate their data could be used to identify the locations of US military bases. “Data privacy is not like a consumer good, where you click ‘I accept’ and all is well. Data privacy is more like air quality or safe drinking water, a public good that cannot be effectively regulated by trusting in the wisdom of millions of individual choices. A more collective response is needed.”

Unfortunately, this also means that you can’t fully safeguard your privacy on your own. You may choose not to purchase Amazon’s ring doorbell, yet you can still show up in the video footage collected by others. You might strengthen your online privacy practices, yet conclusions will still be inferred about you based on the behavior of others. As Professor Tufekci wrote, we need a collective response.

We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
Many people are uncomfortable with surveillance, but feel like they have no say in the matter. While the threats surveillance poses are large, it is not too late to act. We are seeing success: in response to community organizing and an audit, Los Angeles Police Department scrapped a controversial program to predict who is most likely to commit violent crimes. Citizens, researchers, and activists in Detroit have been effective at drawing attention to the Detroit Police Department’s unregulated use of facial recognition and a bill calling for a 5-year moratorium has been introduced to the state legislature. Local governments in San Francisco, Oakland, and Somerville have banned the use of facial recognition by police.

For further resources, please check out: - Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology - Digital Defense Playbook
